true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `downsize` definition silently replaces the (from, to, max_width, max_height) signature

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice: once at line 145 taking `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` and again at line 149 taking `(from, to, dimensions, opts)`. In Ruby the second definition wins, so the 4-positional-argument version no longer exists. Any existing caller that passes width and height (e.g. `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, w, h)`) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments`, and there is no indication all callers were migrated. One of the two definitions must be removed/renamed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size limit hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so images and attachments each respected their configured limits. The change replaces that with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. Sites with `max_attachment_size_kb` above 10MB will now have the client reject attachments the server would accept, and sites with image limits above 10MB get a client-side rejection even though the server can now auto-downsize large images (which is the point of this PR — the client should not pre-emptively block oversized images anymore). The same hardcoding was applied to the 413 handler at line 246.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF downsize passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH

The uploads controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)`. For animated GIFs, `optimize` selects `downsize_instructions_animated`, which delegates to `resize_instructions_animated` and produces `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80% ...`. gifsicle does not accept a percentage for `--resize-fit`; the command fails, `convert_with` returns false, and the retry loop in the controller burns all 5 attempts without shrinking the file. Animated GIFs over the size limit can therefore never be uploaded, and the failure is silent (`&> /dev/null`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Download cap hardcoded to 10MB for API URL uploads

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. While the intent is to allow downloading larger originals for downsizing, this also caps downloads for sites whose configured image limit is above 10MB (they could previously pull larger files), and it downloads full-size originals for non-image types too, with the size magic number duplicated between the controller and the JS client. This should derive from a single setting (e.g. a multiple of max_image_size_kb) rather than a literal.

Downsize retry loop ignores failure and retries identical work

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > limit` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` but never checks its boolean return value. If the conversion fails (bad image, missing convert/gifsicle, unsupported format), the file size never changes and the same failing command is executed 5 times synchronously inside the deferred job before falling through to `Upload.create_for`, which will then fail validation anyway. The result is wasted CPU and a confusing generic error instead of surfacing that the image could not be processed. Break out of the loop when `downsize` returns false.

Downsizing SVGs and other vector/odd formats with `convert -resize 80%` can corrupt or balloon them

The guard uses `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`, which (matching the client-side list) includes SVG. Running ImageMagick `-resize 80%` on an SVG rasterizes it and writes the result over the original path with the `.svg` extension, producing a mislabeled raster file or a failure; repeated attempts can also grow the file, making the loop spin. SVGs (and potentially other formats that don't shrink meaningfully at 80% quality-agnostic resize) should be excluded from the auto-downsize path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes when host is nil

The `before_validation` block calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. If `host` is nil (e.g. the admin submits the create form with a blank host, so `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` is nil in `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host`), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` instead of producing a validation error. Guard with `if self.host.present?`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update and destroy crash on unknown id instead of 404

`EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns nil for a nonexistent id. `update` then calls `save_host(nil)` which raises NoMethodError on `host.host=`, and `destroy` calls `nil.destroy`. Both should raise `Discourse::NotFound` / return 404 when the record is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive host comparison against lower(host)

`record_for_host` queries `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` but never downcases the incoming `host`. A referer like `HTTP://EVILTROUT.COM/page` yields `uri.host == "EVILTROUT.COM"`, which won't match the lowercase stored value, so embedding is wrongly rejected. Use `host.downcase` in the comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents are swapped

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` defines the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` fabricators. The definitions happen to load globally so tests pass, but the files are named for the wrong fabricators, which will confuse anyone editing or looking up fabricators by filename and breaks the convention the test suite relies on. Swap the file contents back.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host values interpolated directly into SQL in migration

The migration builds `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts ... VALUES ('#{h}', ...)` by interpolating `h`, which comes from the admin-editable `embeddable_hosts` site setting. A host entry containing a single quote (or any SQL metacharacters) will produce malformed SQL and abort the migration, and in general this is SQL injection into a migration. Use parameterized execution (e.g. `exec_insert` with binds) or at minimum `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote(h)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category setting row is absent

`execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id']` assumes the query returns at least one row. Site settings only have rows in the `site_settings` table once they've been changed from the default, so any site that never customized `embed_category` (the common case) will get an empty result set, and `[0]` will be `nil`, raising `NoMethodError: undefined method '[]' for nil` and aborting the migration. The same pattern is used for `uncategorized_category_id` on line 15. Both lookups need a nil-safe fallback.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
No uniqueness validation on host

Nothing prevents creating two `EmbeddableHost` rows with the same host (the old site setting was a flat list where duplicates were harmless). Duplicates make `record_for_host` nondeterministic about which category an embedded topic lands in and clutter the admin UI. Add `validates_uniqueness_of :host` (case-insensitive) and ideally a unique index in the migration.

Redundant/duplicated authorization filters

Both new admin controllers declare `before_filter :ensure_logged_in, :ensure_staff`, but `Admin::AdminController` already enforces admin access, and the routes are additionally wrapped in `AdminConstraint`. More notably `ensure_staff` would allow moderators (staff but not admins) while `AdminConstraint` allows admins — the layering is inconsistent; the controllers should rely on the standard admin controller behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TopicUser.find_by can return nil, causing a 500 on unsubscribe

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` is not guaranteed to exist. Users can receive notification emails without ever having a topic_users row for the topic (e.g. mailing-list mode subscribers, or users notified via category watching where the row was never created). In that case `tu.notification_level` on line 107 raises NoMethodError and the unsubscribe link from the email returns a 500. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` which creates the row when missing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Direct save bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

The action mutates `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of `TopicUser.change`. As a result `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not set, and no `notification_level_change` message is published on MessageBus, so any open browser tabs of that user keep showing the old notification state and reporting that relies on the changed-at/reason fields is wrong. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` for consistency with every other code path that changes notification levels.

No controller/request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The PR adds a state-changing endpoint (`topics#unsubscribe`), new routes, and a mailer link, but the only spec change is adding an `unsubscribe_url` option to an existing message-builder test. There is no coverage for the redirect-on-slug-mismatch branch, the level-downgrade/mute logic, the nil TopicUser case, or the requirement that the user be logged in — all of which contain bugs noted above.

Unsubscribe mutates notification state on a plain GET request

The new `unsubscribe` action is exposed via GET (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) and immediately changes the user's `notification_level` in the database before rendering. GET requests are issued without user intent by mail-client link prefetchers, virus scanners (e.g. Outlook SafeLinks), and browser prerendering, and they carry no CSRF protection. Any such automated fetch of the unsubscribe URL will silently mute/change the user's topic subscription. Unsubscribe-via-GET should either require a POST confirmation or at minimum not apply the state change until the user confirms on the rendered page.

Watching/tracking users are demoted to 'regular', still receiving notifications

The logic sets the level to `regular` when it is currently above regular, and only mutes when it is regular or below. A user watching a topic (the most common reason for getting email) who clicks 'stop receiving notifications about this topic' is moved to regular, under which they still receive reply/mention notifications. The email copy ('To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here') and the page text ('You will stop receiving notifications') then claim the opposite of what happened.

ensure_logged_in blocks the email unsubscribe flow for logged-out users

`unsubscribe` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` filter list. The feature's entry point is a link in a notification email, and recipients frequently are not logged in (mobile mail clients, different browser). Those users are bounced to the login page and, even after logging in, are not taken back to the unsubscribe URL, so the one-click unsubscribe silently fails for exactly the audience it targets. Consider a signed token in the unsubscribe URL (like the existing digest unsubscribe key) instead of requiring a session.

unsubscribe_link now requires %{unsubscribe_url} but not all callers pass it

The `unsubscribe_link` translation now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` in `Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` is invoked for every email built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`; any current or future caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link` without passing `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. plugins, or the spec's own builder which previously only used `add_unsubscribe_link: true`) will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and the email will fail to send. Either make the per-topic sentence conditional on the URL being present or guard against the missing key.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match statistics update is racy and performed inside a validation

should_block? reads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, and saves, which loses increments under concurrent signups; more notably it is called from EmailValidator#validate_each, so merely validating a User (not saving) performs a database write with `record.save`, whose failure is silently ignored. Use an atomic update (e.g. update_counters / UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) and consider moving the stats update out of the validation path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email check is case-sensitive and easily bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` lookup, and the value passed here is the raw `user.email` attribute, which is stored as the user typed it (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] directly, no downcasing). A blocked address like spammer@example.com can register as Spammer@Example.com and sail past the block list, since PostgreSQL string comparison is case-sensitive. The email should be normalized (e.g. Email.downcase) before the lookup, both here and wherever BlockedEmail records are created.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocked emails not enforced on change_email

The new BlockedEmail validation only runs via User's `email` validator, but `change_email` never saves the user with the new email — it only checks uniqueness and creates an email token; the token confirmation path (EmailToken.confirm) updates the address without going through the new validator. An existing account (or one created before an address was blocked) can switch to a blocked email address, defeating the feature. The block check should also be applied in the email-change flow.

rejectedEmails comparison is exact-string and won't match case variants

After a failed signup the server echoes back result.values.email and it is pushed into rejectedEmails; the check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` is an exact string comparison against the current accountEmail input. If the user retries with different casing (e.g. Bad@Spam.com vs bad@spam.com) the client-side rejection won't trigger and they'll get another full server round-trip each time. Compare lowercased values.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that merely appears as a substring of discourseUrl. An origin like `https://evil.com/redirect?https://forum.example.com` would pass if discourseUrl is configured correspondingly, and more simply the check never validates that e.origin actually equals the forum's origin. Any site able to get a message to the parent window can resize the iframe; the check should compare e.origin against a parsed expected origin.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content can be nil, crashing the hourly feed job

In poll_feed, `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has a `content` element. Plain RSS 2.0 feeds typically only have `description`, not `content`, so SimpleRSS will return nil and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the entire feed poll (and because `sidekiq_options retry: false`, nothing is retried and no items from that feed are imported until the next hour, which will crash the same way). Use `i.content || i.description` and guard for nil.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Check-then-create on embed_url races and raises RecordNotUnique

import() does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then `TopicEmbed.create!` inside a transaction. The migration adds a unique index on embed_url, so two concurrent imports of the same URL (hourly PollFeed plus a RetrieveTopic job enqueued from embed#best, which explicitly runs PollFeed and then fetches HTTP itself) will both find no row and one will crash with ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique. Rescue RecordNotUnique and fall back to the update path, or use an upsert.

Editing an already-shipped migration to add force: true

CreateTopTopics already ran in existing deployments; changing `create_table :top_topics` to `force: true` modifies history. Environments that haven't run it yet (or that replay migrations, e.g. some CI/staging rebuilds after a partially applied state) will silently DROP and recreate the top_topics table, losing all aggregated counts. New behavior should go in a new migration rather than editing an old one.

Throws if #discourse-comments element is missing

`comments.appendChild(iframe)` runs without checking that `document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` found an element. Site owners paste this snippet into arbitrary templates; if the container is absent or renamed, the script throws and no iframe is created, with no useful error. Bail out early (or log a clear message) when comments is null.

X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL is non-standard and unsupported

`response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = 'ALLOWALL'` is not a valid X-Frame-Options value (ALLOW-FROM requires a URI and is unsupported in Chrome/Safari; ALLOWALL is ignored entirely by most browsers). The effect is only achieved because an invalid value happens to be ignored — better to explicitly remove the header so the intent is clear and future middleware adding a default DENY doesn't break embeds.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

Any href/src starting with '/' is prefixed with the article's scheme+host. Protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/x.jpg` start with '/', so they are rewritten to `http://host/cdn.example.com/x.jpg`, breaking those links/images in every imported post. Check for a leading '//' and skip (or prepend only the scheme) before treating the URL as host-relative.

feed_key is dead code; job does no change detection

feed_key computes a redis key 'feed-modified:<sha>' but nothing ever reads or writes it, and poll_feed re-downloads the feed and re-hashes/re-imports every item every hour. Either wire the key up to skip unchanged feeds (e.g. via If-Modified-Since/ETag or content hash) or remove it; as-is every hourly run re-fetches all items and calls PostRevisor/sha comparisons for each.

import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` appends the 'imported from' footer directly to the string passed in. Callers that reuse the buffer (e.g. the Readability document content or anything comparing the original afterwards) get silently modified data, and the sha1 is computed over the mutated value. Duplicate the string (`contents = contents + ...` or `contents.dup`) before appending.

raw_html cook method stores and serves completely unsanitized HTML

`cook` returns `raw` verbatim when cook_method is :raw_html, so posts imported via TopicEmbed.import (feed polling or remote retrieval of the embeddable host) bypass PrettyText/Sanitize entirely and are served as-is (the embed view even does `raw post.cooked`). Any script/event-handler markup in a fetched article or feed item becomes stored XSS on the forum itself, visible in topic pages, digests, and embeds. The imported HTML should be run through Sanitize with an allowlist before storage.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits non-existent -ms-align-items property

The new align-items mixin includes `-ms-align-items: $alignment;` (line 121). There is no such property: IE10/11 only support the 2012 syntax `-ms-flex-align`, which is already emitted on the previous line. The bogus declaration is silently ignored by browsers, so it is dead output in every compiled stylesheet that uses the mixin; it should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
.valign-helper rule is now dead code after flexbox switch

.d-header .contents is now a flex container with align-items: center, which makes the .valign-helper element (display: inline-block; height: 100%; vertical-align: middle) — a hack for vertical centering in inline-block layouts — completely ineffective, since vertical-align has no effect on flex items and height: 100% inside a flex row behaves differently. The rule (and the corresponding markup, if any) should be removed to avoid confusion.

float: right on .small-action button no longer works inside new flex container

The PR turns .small-action into a flex container (@include flexbox()), but the button inside it still relies on `float: right` (line ~309) to be pushed to the right edge. CSS floats are ignored on flex items, so the button will now render immediately after the .small-action-desc content instead of being right-aligned. The same applies to the leftover `float: left` declarations on .topic-avatar and .small-action-desc .avatar. The layout should be expressed with flex properties (e.g. margin-left: auto on the button) or the floats removed, otherwise the small-action row layout regresses.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix, so AMS never calls it

ActiveModelSerializers filters attributes via methods named `include_<attr>?`. The new method is defined as `def include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is never invoked and `website_name` is always serialized — including as `nil` when the user has no website. The intended guard (`website.present?`) has no effect. Rename it to `include_website_name?`.

false_positives.candidate:
Query string and fragment are dropped from displayed website name

When the domains match, the display value is built as `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path`, discarding any query string or fragment. A user whose website is `http://example.com/page?id=5` on the same host will see it displayed as `example.com/page`, which no longer represents the actual URL. Include `URI#query`/`fragment` or use `request_uri` when constructing the display path.

website_name is not declared an untrusted attribute, leaking TL0 users' websites to anonymous viewers

The serializer hides `website` from anonymous viewers of TL0 users via `untrusted_attributes :website, ...`, but the newly added `website_name` attribute is not in that list. Since `website_name` is derived directly from `website`, an anonymous visitor can now read a TL0 user's website host (and path) from the `website_name` field even though `website` itself is correctly suppressed. Add `website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (and fix the missing `?` on its include method).

website_name returns nil for websites without a scheme or with unparseable URLs

`URI(website.to_s).host rescue nil` returns nil for values like `example.com/user` (no scheme — URI parses it as a path, host is nil) or any malformed URL that survives profile validation, causing `website_name` to be nil and the template's `{{#if model.website_name}}` to hide the website link entirely even though `model.website` is present. Previously the client-side code displayed `website.split('/')[2]`, which also degraded, but the new serializer should fall back to the raw `website` string instead of returning nil so the link remains visible.

true_positives.golden_comment: In .topic-meta-data h5 a, the original code had color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) but was changed to dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)). The lightness for the light theme changed from 30% to 70%, which is a dramatic inversion
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Light-theme color changed from 30% to 70% lightness for embedded post meta-data link

The original rule was `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The replacement is `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`, so on light themes the color shifts from a 30%-lightened $primary to a 70%-lightened $primary, making the bold poster-name link in expanded embedded posts much fainter than before. The dark arm (30% of $secondary) is the correct dark-theme counterpart of the original 30%; the light arm should have stayed 30%.

true_positives.golden_comment: This change for desktop/user.css changes $primary from 30% to 50% for the light theme; most other changes preserve the original $primary value and move the complement to $secondary for dark. Consider reviewing this (also applies to a similar .name change in the mobile variant).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
group-member-info .name light-theme color changed from 30% to 50% lightness

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
@loaded_locales is read outside the load mutex and can be nil on first translate

In `translate`, `@loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)` is evaluated without synchronization and without the nil guard that the newly added `ensure_loaded!` has (`@loaded_locales ||= []`). `@loaded_locales` is only initialized in `reload!`; if `translate` is invoked before any `reload!` (or after a direct `load_locale` call from another thread partially completes), the first check raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil`. More generally the check-then-load pattern here is unsynchronized, so two threads can race through `load_locale` — the mutex inside `load_locale` makes the double-load harmless, but the nil read is not protected. `translate` should use the same `@loaded_locales ||= []` guard (or route through `ensure_loaded!`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Custom fallback list drops parent-language fallbacks for regional locales (e.g. pt_BR no longer falls back to pt)

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` returns exactly `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]`. The standard `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` behavior (which `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` provided and this PR removes) decomposes regional locales so that `pt_BR` falls back to `pt` before hitting the default. With this change, a user with locale `pt_BR` (or `zh_TW`, `nb_NO`-style tags) will see English for every key that exists in the base `pt` translation but not in `pt_BR`, which is a user-visible regression for regional locales. The TODO comment even acknowledges per-language ordering is needed; at minimum the list should insert the language-only parent (`locale.to_s.split('_').first`) between the locale and the site default.

Fallback locales are only loaded during controller requests, so fallback translations are missing in jobs/mailers

The new fallback mechanism depends on `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` being called to eagerly load the user's locale, `SiteSetting.default_locale`, and `:en` (because the translate accelerator only lazy-loads `config.locale`). This call was added only in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any code path that translates outside of a controller request — Sidekiq/scheduled jobs, email rendering (`UserNotifications`), oneboxing, rake tasks, console — will translate with only the current locale's yml loaded. When a key is missing in that locale, the fallbacks backend looks up the default locale and `:en`, finds nothing loaded, and renders 'translation missing' instead of the English fallback. `ensure_loaded!` needs to be invoked wherever `I18n.locale=` is set (e.g., in the jobs/mailer code paths), not just in the controller.

FallbackLocaleList recomputes SiteSetting.default_locale on every translation fallback lookup

Because `FallbackLocaleList#[]` is overridden without memoization, every translation lookup that misses the primary locale triggers a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read (which hits the site settings cache/provider) and allocates a new array. Under load this happens per missing-key translation. Consider caching the computed list per locale (e.g., storing into the Hash) and invalidating when the default locale setting changes.

BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets, changing prev-cursor semantics

The change in BasePaginator.get_result replaces `results = queryset[offset:stop]` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, a negative offset was previously impossible to reach successfully (Django would raise), so clamping changes behavior silently for all users of Paginator/DateTimePaginator codebase-wide: a client-supplied negative-offset cursor that used to fail loudly now returns the first page as if offset were 0, while the cursor arithmetic later (`_build_next_values` uses the raw `cursor.offset`) still computes next offsets from the original negative offset, producing inconsistent cursors. If clamping is intended, it should be applied uniformly (and probably rejected with BadPaginationError instead), not papered over only in the slice.

Given that both the datetime key handling and the negative-slice behavior are broken as noted, unit tests covering first-page, next-page, prev-page, and malformed-cursor cases for OptimizedCursorPaginator, plus an endpoint test with optimized_pagination=true, are required before merging.

The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. If that is the case here, the paginator will always be constructed with `enable_advanced_features=False` (or paginate will raise TypeError for the unexpected kwarg), and the new code path is dead. This needs a test verifying the flag actually reaches OptimizedCursorPaginator.

Negative-offset path in OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on Django querysets

Django's QuerySet explicitly disallows negative slicing (`Negative indexing is not supported` AssertionError), so instead of 'the ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' as the comment claims, any request that exercises this path returns a 500. Since cursor offsets are parsed from the client-supplied cursor string (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative integers), a superuser on the audit log endpoint can trigger this with a crafted cursor. The feature is both broken and untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Redirect-follow loop limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop that follows span-id redirects was changed from 10000 to 1000 iterations. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will now stop resolving early, so a span is attached to an intermediate set instead of the true root set, splitting one segment into multiple flushed segments (and leaving stale redirect entries). The previous code's comment explicitly warned about this failure mode at 10k; lowering the bound makes silent mis-grouping 10x more likely with no compensating metric or error when the limit is hit.

max_segment_spans guard removed while Lua cap is hardcoded and inconsistent

The `_load_segment_data` span-count safety check (`max_segment_spans`) was deleted and replaced by a hardcoded `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. Two problems: (1) the configurable `max_segment_spans=1001` constructor parameter is now dead code and no longer enforced anywhere; (2) eviction only happens inside the Lua script, so spans inserted via the initial `zadd` pipeline in `process_spans` (which runs before the script per batch) or races between consumers can still grow a set beyond the cap and will now be flushed unbounded, since the load-time check that previously dropped oversized segments is gone. Oversized segments can again produce multi-thousand-span Kafka messages.

zpopmin evicts earliest-ending spans, biasing segment contents

The eviction uses `zpopmin`, which removes the spans with the lowest score (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`). For a segment that exceeds 1000 spans this silently drops the oldest spans rather than the newest, which is the opposite of what one would typically want (keeping the root/earliest spans preserves segment structure), and dropped spans vanish with no metric or log, making the loss invisible in production.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python's hash(), which is randomized per process

The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples/strings is salted by PYTHONHASHSEED, so it produces different values in every process and every restart. Two workers handling the same organization/projects will compute different keys, so the 'performance optimization' cache is almost never hit across processes, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (which recomputes the key the same way) will delete a different key than the one that was set if called in another process, making invalidation silently ineffective. Use a deterministic serialization of the sorted project IDs (e.g. join with commas or hashlib.md5).

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility checks outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` but the upsampling check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` with the closure-captured outer `dataset`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` (or the split dataset) while the outer dataset may be `metrics_performance`, and vice versa. The eligibility decision therefore reflects the wrong dataset: error-focused queries executed against `discover` for a split widget will not be upsampled (outer dataset is metrics), producing undercounted error counts in dashboard widgets, and a transactions-scoped query could incorrectly be upsampled if the outer dataset is `errors`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule checked in

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (subproject commit a5d29095...) pointing at the repository's own base commit. This looks like an accidentally committed nested checkout/submodule; it will break clones for anyone without the submodule configured and bloat the repo. It should be removed from the PR.

Error detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query string, missing split/negated queries

`_is_error_focused_query` inspects `request.GET.get("query")` for the substring 'event.type:error'. This misses error-only queries that don't literally contain that substring — most notably the dashboard split path in organization_events_stats.py builds `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"`, which is errors-only but never matches, so those error timeseries are not upsampled. It can also false-positive on a query like `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. The decision should be based on the query actually being executed (and ideally on parsed search filters), not raw GET text.

setUp overwrites self.user after login_as, breaking the authenticated session

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` is called first, then `self.user = self.create_user()` and `self.user2 = self.create_user()` reassign the attributes. The session is authenticated as the original user, but the events are tagged with the new (different) users, and any test behavior depending on `self.user` being the logged-in user is wrong. The new-user creation should happen before `login_as`, or the pre-existing `self.user` from the base TestCase should be reused.

upsampled_count truncates with toInt64 instead of rounding

The `upsampled_count` function wraps `sum(sample_weight)` in `toInt64`, which truncates toward zero. Sample weights derived from client sample rates are floats (e.g. 1/0.1 = 10.0 but 1/0.3 = 3.333...), so aggregated counts can be systematically under-reported whenever the summed weight lands just below an integer. Consider `toInt64(round(sum(sample_weight)))` so fractional accumulation rounds to the nearest count.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutual-exclusion validation uses truthiness so age=0 or timestamp=0 bypasses the check

`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get('age')` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get('timestamp')`. Both `age` and `timestamp` are integers where 0 is a legitimate value (age of 0 milliseconds, epoch timestamp 0). A report containing both `timestamp` and `age: 0` (or `timestamp: 0` and `age`) will pass validation even though the spec says they are mutually exclusive, because `0` is falsy. The check should test key presence (`'age' in self.initial_data`) rather than truthiness.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

false_positives.candidate:
Chronological merge compares error event timestamps against segment event timestamps with a silent 0 default

In `gen_request_data`, the code interleaves error log messages with breadcrumb log messages by comparing `error_events[error_idx]['timestamp'] < event.get('timestamp', 0)`. Segment events that lack a `timestamp` key default to 0, which causes all remaining error messages to be flushed before those events regardless of when the errors actually occurred, silently corrupting the chronological ordering sent to Seer. Additionally, the two timestamp sources (nodestore event `timestamp` and recording-segment event `timestamp`) are assumed to be on the same clock/units; if they differ, the merged ordering will be wrong. At minimum, events without a timestamp should be handled explicitly instead of defaulting to 0.

get_environment_info performs a recommended-event lookup per issue when building PR comments

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the merged-PR comment list (up to 5 issues per comment, run for each PR on each deployment). Each call hits the eventstore/nodestore, so generating one comment issues a sequence of per-issue queries inline in the PR comment task. If the recommended event lookup is expensive or times out, comment delivery is delayed (the broad `except Exception` also masks real failures by design, so problems will be invisible). Consider batching the event fetches or using a cheaper source of the environment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic

The login flow decrypts the code list, checks `indexOf`, and then updates the user row in a separate, non-transactional step. Two concurrent login requests presenting the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either writes back, allowing a single-use code to be used twice. The copy in the UI explicitly promises each code "can be used exactly once". Consider an atomic update or a conditional update keyed on the stored value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes unusable for Google/SAML users with 2FA

In the credentials authorize flow, the identity-provider guards run before the backup-code branch and only check `credentials.totpCode`: `user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode` throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled, and `!user.password && ... && !credentials.totpCode` throws IncorrectEmailPassword. A Google/SAML user with 2FA enabled who loses their authenticator and submits a backup code (the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow sends no totpCode) will be rejected before the backup-code check at line 131 is ever reached, and such users also have no password to fall back on. The guards should also pass when `credentials.backupCode` is present.

No test coverage for logging in with a backup code

The PR's core security feature — consuming a backup code during login and enforcing single-use — has no test. The added tests only cover the download/copy buttons on the setup screen, and the file itself acknowledges this with a TODO. A regression in the authorize backup-code branch (e.g. the identity-provider guard issue) would not be caught.

missing_backup_codes message instructs an impossible action

The new string "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." tells users to generate backup codes in settings, but this PR adds no way to (re)generate backup codes from settings — codes are only created during initial 2FA setup. A user who hits this error (e.g. 2FA enabled before this feature existed, so `backupCodes` is null) is directed to an action that does not exist.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback lookup compares externalCalendarId to itself and can never match

In `updateEvent` (and the identical pattern in `deleteEvent` at line 317), the fallback when `externalCalendarId` is falsy is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. Searching for a calendar whose externalId equals the (falsy) externalCalendarId can never succeed, so `selectedCalendar` becomes `undefined` and `calendar.events.update` is called with `calendarId: undefined`, failing the API call. Previously the fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, which resolved to the host's calendar. The intent appears to be matching the destination calendar against the credential in use, similar to what `createEvent` now does with `credentialId`; as written, updates/deletes for bookings whose reference has no `externalCalendarId` will silently break.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated logic inversion in organization slug persistence

This PR about destinationCalendar arrays also changes organization creation: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` became `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting when the org slug is stored on the team record. This is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose, untested, and changes which deployments persist `slug` vs `requestedSlug` — if unintentional it will break org subdomain resolution; if intentional it belongs in its own PR with justification.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
createEvent always uses the first destination calendar regardless of which host's credential is used

`Office365CalendarService.createEvent` destructures `event.destinationCalendar[0]` and posts to `/me/calendars/{firstCalendar.externalId}/events`. With this PR, `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` now calls `createEvent` once per host credential for collective events, but the service signature was not updated to accept the credentialId/externalId being processed (unlike Google, which received a `credentialId` parameter and picks the matching calendar). For a collective booking, host B's Office365 credential will try to create the event in host A's calendar (whose externalId is meaningless to host B's account), so the call fails or creates the event in the wrong place. The same problem exists in `LarkCalendarService` and `BaseCalendarService` (caldav), which also only ever look at `destinationCalendar[0]`. The per-credential calendar must be selected the same way Google's implementation does.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One unresolvable reference aborts updates for all remaining calendar references

In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, if a reference has a `credentialId` that is neither in `this.calendarCredentials` nor found in the DB (deleted credential, or a credential belonging to a collective host that no longer exists), `credential` stays `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still pushed into `result`. `updateEvent` calls `getCalendar(undefined)`, which throws; the outer try/catch then swallows everything and returns failure results for all references — so a single stale reference prevents updating every other host's calendar event on reschedule. The loop should skip references whose credential cannot be resolved (with a logged warning) instead of pushing the update.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

false_positives.candidate:
Collective hosts' destination calendars are dropped when the organizer has none

The new code sets `destinationCalendar` to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, and later does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. If the organizer has no destination calendar but other collective hosts do, the optional-chained push is a no-op and the hosts' calendars are silently discarded — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix (hosts not getting invited). The collective branch should initialize the array, e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`.

Crash when destinationCalendar is empty/null and location is Google Meet

In `EventManager.create`, the new code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. When the event has no destination calendar (null or empty array — common for users with no connected calendar), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError. Previously this line used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`), so it was safe. Any booking with location `integrations:google:meet` and no destination calendar will now fail during event creation. The check should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

No tests cover the new multi-host destinationCalendar behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". This change alters the `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` contract from a single object to an array and rewires create/update/delete paths across Google, Office365, Lark, CalDAV, EventManager, cancellation, rescheduling, and payment webhooks — including subtle per-credential calendar selection and booking reference persistence (`referencesToCreate` now uses `result.externalId`/`result.credentialId`). Given regressions like the empty-array crash in `EventManager.create` and the Office365 first-calendar-only behavior, at minimum unit tests for `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` with multiple hosts and for the no-destination-calendar case should be required before merging.

Recurring-event deletes now run once per calendar reference, causing duplicated delete calls

The recurring-cancellation branch (delete all remaining bookings' events across all the user's calendar credentials) was moved inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. For a collective booking with two calendar references, the block that iterates over every user credential and every updated booking is executed once per reference, so each event is deleted N times (and `apiDeletes` collects duplicates). Besides wasted API calls, some providers error on deleting an already-deleted event. Additionally, the inner loop still only deletes `updBooking.references.find(...)` — the first calendar reference per booking — so extra hosts' references are never removed. The recurring-delete block should run once outside the per-reference loop, and should iterate over all calendar references of each updated booking.

hangoutLink patch uses undefined calendarId when fallback "primary" was used for insert

In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent `calendar.events.patch` that adds the hangout link uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the fallback. When no destination calendar matches the credentialId (selectedCalendar is undefined), the event is created on "primary" but the follow-up patch is issued with `calendarId: undefined`, so the description with the Meet link is never written (and the promise rejection is unhandled). Apply the same `|| "primary"` fallback to the patch call.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema corrupts stored credentials: computed keys don't do what's intended, unknown fields are stripped, and a fake refresh_token is injected

In zod, computed keys in an object literal like `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` do not create a catch-all rule for 'any property that is a number'; they just produce a literal (garbage) key. So in sync mode the schema effectively becomes `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), ... })`, which (a) strips every other field from the parsed result by default — so `refreshTokenResponse.data` returned to callers contains only `access_token`, dropping `expiry_date`/`expires_in`/scope that callers then persist (e.g. Google stores the result via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, wiping the real refresh token and expiry from the credential), and (b) line 26 then writes the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token when none is present, permanently corrupting the stored credential so subsequent real refreshes fail with invalid_grant.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync endpoint response is returned as a raw fetch Response without checking status or parsing the body

When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and returns the raw `Response` object. It never checks `response.ok` and never calls `response.json()`. Callers then break: for example `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;` — a fetch Response has no `.data`, so this throws TypeError whenever sync mode is on. Similarly office365video/webex call `handleErrorsJson(response)` and others call `await resp.json()`, which would consume the body of an un-checked response. Token refresh silently fails for every integration when the feature is enabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Passes credentialId instead of the Cal.com userId to refreshOAuthTokens

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's database id as the third argument, but that parameter is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. The parent platform will receive a credential id instead of a user id and will either 404 or refresh tokens for the wrong user. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this one should capture `credential.userId` in biginAuth and pass that.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zod parse and decrypt errors bubble up as unhandled 500s

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`, `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw on invalid input (malformed body, wrong encryption key, non-JSON plaintext). Since the handler has no try/catch, callers get an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400; a misconfigured sender has no way to distinguish bad payload from server failure, and the webhook sender will likely retry forever.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string equality

The header value is compared to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` using `!==`. This is a timing-safe-comparison candidate: use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) for a shared secret guarding credential writes. Additionally the secret check does not guard against both values being empty strings in a misconfigured deployment (empty header === empty env passes), and there is no method restriction or rate limiting on an endpoint that writes OAuth credentials.

findFirst-then-create race allows duplicate credentials for the same user/app

The endpoint does `findFirst` and then `create` without a transaction or unique constraint on (userId, appId). Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app both miss the findFirst and both create, leaving two credentials where downstream code uses `findFirst` and silently picks one. Use `prisma.credential.upsert` on a unique compound key (add one if missing) or wrap in a transaction with serializable isolation.

isExpired compares expiry_date against +new Date() (milliseconds) but other services use seconds — unchanged inconsistency now matters more

`isExpired = (expiryDate) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())` is correct here because expiry_date is stored in ms in this file, but office365calendar's own service stores `expires_in` in seconds and compares against seconds. With credentials now being pushed in from an external platform via the webhook, the expiry semantics (seconds vs ms) of the synced keys are undocumented and differ per integration, so externally-synced credentials will be treated as expired (or never expiring) depending on the app. The sync contract in the PR description only says 'access token and expiry date' without specifying units.

prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService

The new getClient code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time error (and a runtime ReferenceError if it were to build), so the Salesforce calendar service is broken by this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist check is case-sensitive and easily bypassed

`BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` entries are lowercased, but the incoming guest email is compared without lowercasing: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. A blacklisted address like `spam@example.com` can be added as `Spam@Example.com` and bypass the blacklist entirely. The guest email should be normalized (e.g. `guest.toLowerCase()`) before the comparison (and ideally before the duplicate-attendee comparison too, since email matching against existing attendees is also case-sensitive).

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check uses && instead of ||, blocking team admins

The permission check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. This only passes for a user who is simultaneously a team admin AND a team owner, so regular team admins (who are not owners) get FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to team bookings. This should be an OR: `isTeamAdmin(...) || isTeamOwner(...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Clicking Add with only the default empty field shows a validation error

`multiEmailValue` is initialized to `[""]`, so its length is 1, not 0. If the user opens the dialog and clicks Add without typing anything, `safeParse` fails on the empty string and the user sees the red 'Emails must be unique and valid' error instead of the action being a no-op. Empty strings should be filtered out before the length check and validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email-disable settings

Every other sender in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, etc.) respects `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail` so organizers can disable standard emails via event type metadata. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata parameter and unconditionally emails the organizer, all team members, and all attendees, so guests-added emails are sent even when the event type is configured to suppress standard emails.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New-guest detection can fail due to email casing mismatch

`newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` compares the raw user input against stored attendee emails. If the entered email differs in case from what was stored, a newly added guest receives the 'existing attendee' AttendeeAddGuestsEmail instead of the AttendeeScheduledEmail with full booking details, and conversely an existing attendee could be mis-classified. Compare case-insensitively.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar attendee update uses the requester's credentials, not the organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` builds the EventManager with the calling user's credentials. But attendees are allowed to call this endpoint (`isAttendee` passes the permission check), and an attendee typically has no credentials for the organizer's calendar, so `updateCalendarAttendees` will either no-op or update the wrong calendar. The calendar event lives on the organizer's calendar, so the organizer's credentials (already partially loaded via `booking.user.credentials`) should be used.

No check that the booking is in a valid state before adding guests

The handler fetches the booking by id but never checks `booking.status`. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings (and past bookings), and both the calendar update (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) and the emails send an ICS with `status: "CONFIRMED"` and method `REQUEST`, re-inviting people to a cancelled event. The handler should reject bookings that are cancelled/rejected (and arguably past).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount incremented via stale read-modify-write instead of atomic increment

Both failure paths set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched at the start of the run. If two cron executions overlap (or the row is otherwise updated between the findMany and the update), one increment is lost, so a reminder that should be deleted after two failures survives for extra runs. Prisma supports `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which is atomic and immune to the stale read; it should be used in both the `else` branch (line ~184) and the `catch` block (line ~195).

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` in the deleteMany has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the sibling branch. WorkflowReminder rows are shared across EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP methods, so any non-SMS reminder that ever gets retryCount > 1 (e.g., if the email cron adopts the same retry pattern, or via manual/data-fix updates) will be silently deleted by the SMS cron. The method filter should be applied to the whole OR (or duplicated in the retryCount branch) to keep this cron from touching other reminder types.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded retryCount update in catch block can crash the whole cron run

The catch handler now performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` before logging. If that update itself throws (e.g., the database error that caused the original exception persists, or the row was concurrently deleted), the exception propagates out of the for-loop, the handler returns a 500, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are skipped for this run. The update in the catch block should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or the failure recorded without a second awaited DB call) so one failing reminder cannot abort processing of the rest.
