This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching behavior tests removed without replacement

The two 'Caching' describe-block tests verifying that getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions return cached results on second invocation were deleted. The caching logic still exists in the service (cachedAuthConditions / cachedFilterConditions), so this regression coverage is lost; a bug that drops caching would silently cause repeated DB membership lookups per query. Re-add equivalent tests against the new Prisma.Sql return values.

findMany method removed, breaking existing callers

The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method on InsightsBookingService was deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any existing caller that invoked `service.findMany({ select: ... })` to query `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized` will now fail to compile (or at runtime), and callers must now hand-write `$queryRaw` SQL against the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table themselves, duplicating table/column knowledge outside the service. The PR does not update or mention any call sites. Either keep a `findMany`-style query method in the service or update/migrate all consumers in this PR.

getBaseConditions integration test asserts exact result set without ORDER BY and without isolating other rows

The test runs `SELECT id FROM "BookingTimeStatusDenormalized" WHERE ${baseConditions}` and asserts `results` equals exactly `[{ id: userBooking.id }]`. The denormalized table is populated asynchronously from Booking rows in production-like setups; the test creates rows in `Booking` but never verifies/writes the denormalized rows, so the query may return zero rows (or stale rows from other test data matching the same user/eventType) making the assertion flaky. Also, without ORDER BY, any multi-row match has nondeterministic ordering for a strict toEqual on an array. The test should either write directly to the denormalized table or tolerate ordering (e.g., expect.arrayContaining / sorted comparison).

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' syntax only works on macOS, script fails on Linux

Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E ...`, which is the BSD/macOS sed syntax. On GNU sed (Linux), `-i ''` is interpreted as editing a file literally named `''` and the command fails, so GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is never updated on Linux dev machines or containers. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm file.bak`) or detect the platform.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp hardcoded to en-US locale, ignoring user's locale

The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, so every user sees US-style dates (M/D/YY, 12-hour time) regardless of their configured locale, unlike the rest of the app which formats dates per user preference. Pass the user's locale (available via `useLocale` / i18n language) to `Intl.DateTimeFormat` instead of the hardcoded "en-US".

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:
ENV_FILE relative path breaks depending on invocation directory

`ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's current working directory, not the script's location. Running the script from the repo root (the natural way: `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) resolves to a `.env` one level above the repo and silently creates/updates the wrong file. Resolve the path from the script's own directory, e.g. `ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)/.env"`.

deleteCache mutation never invalidates connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in UI

The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` callback, but unlike `disconnectMutation` right below it, it has no `onSettled` that invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. After a user deletes the cache, the `cacheUpdatedAt` value rendered in this same dropdown still comes from the old query data, so the dropdown keeps showing 'Cache Status / Last updated' and the delete option even though the cache rows were just deleted. If the parent doesn't pass an `onChanged` that refetches (it's optional), the stale state persists indefinitely. Add `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` on success/settled for the delete-cache mutation.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path in deleteScheduledEmailReminder never deletes or flags the WorkflowReminder row

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` (used here for workflow deletion and deleted steps, and in handleNewBooking for reschedules) cancels the send at SendGrid but then returns without deleting the WorkflowReminder row or setting `cancelled=true`. For workflow/step deletion the rows are removed by the onDelete: Cascade, but for the reschedule call site in handleNewBooking the rows survive with `scheduled=true, cancelled=false` until their scheduledDate passes and the cron's generic deleteMany removes them — meanwhile nothing in the system knows their SendGrid send is already cancelled. Either delete the row in the immediateDelete branch or set `cancelled=true` so state stays consistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation query lacks method filter and only covers a 1-hour window, so a missed cron run can leak sends

The `remindersToCancel` query filters only on `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now + 1h` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` filter and no `referenceId` non-null check. It works today only because no other code path sets `cancelled=true` for SMS reminders; that implicit coupling is fragile. More importantly, the design relies on the cron running at least once every hour: if the cron is down or delayed beyond the 1-hour window after a reminder is flagged cancelled, the reminder's scheduledDate passes, the first `deleteMany` in the same handler removes the row without ever posting the SendGrid cancellation, and SendGrid delivers the email for a cancelled booking. Consider also cancelling already-due cancelled reminders before the deleteMany (or making the deleteMany exclude `cancelled: true` rows).

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts all remaining cancellations and silently drops the queued DB deletes

In the new cancellation block of the cron handler, the loop awaits `client.request` for each cancelled reminder and collects `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises into `workflowRemindersToDelete`, awaiting them only after the loop. If any single SendGrid request throws (e.g. batch_id already gone, rate limit, network error), the loop exits immediately: (1) all remaining cancelled reminders are not cancelled at SendGrid this run, and (2) the delete promises already collected are never awaited — Prisma promises are lazy, so those rows are never deleted. The rows already cancelled at SendGrid but not deleted will be re-cancelled on the next run (harmless but noisy), while rows not yet reached keep their scheduled emails alive. Each reminder's cancel+delete should be isolated in its own try/catch, and the DB delete should be awaited per reminder.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach makes calendar/video deletions fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch

In `Reschedule`, the loop over `bookingRefsFiltered` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` because `getCalendar` is now async. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so all `calendar.deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` calls are now unawaited: the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns `true` before deletions finish, and any rejection inside a callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection that the surrounding `try/catch` (which only catches synchronous errors) will never see. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (optionally with per-item catch) so failures are logged and deletions complete before the email is sent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Debug log of CalendarService constructor left in getCalendar

`log.info("calendarApp", calendarApp.lib.CalendarService)` logs the CalendarService class constructor on every calendar resolution. This runs on every booking/availability call, adding noisy, low-value log output (and potentially expensive serialization of a class). It looks like a debugging leftover and should be removed or downgraded.

Recurring-cancellation branch pushes into apiDeletes asynchronously after it is awaited

In the recurring-event cancellation path, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes deletion promises into `apiDeletes` from async callbacks. `apiDeletes` is later consumed by `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (and by `await apiDeletes` in the paid branch), both of which run before any of these pushes happen, so the recurring calendar event deletions are never awaited and their results/errors are lost. Cancel can return success while the recurring events remain on the calendar. Collect the deletions with `Promise.all(credentials.map(...))` and push the resulting promises synchronously.

appStore values are now Promises; only 6 of its consumers were updated

Every entry in the default-exported `appStore` map changed from a module namespace object to a `Promise` via top-level `import(...)`. This is a breaking contract change for every consumer of `@calcom/app-store`, but the PR only updates `getCalendar.ts`, `videoClient.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts`, `bookings.tsx`, `deletePayment.ts`, and `handlePayment.ts`. Any other file that indexes `appStore[...]` synchronously (e.g. `appStore[appName].lib` or `appStore[key].app`) will now receive a Promise and silently fail checks like `"lib" in app` or crash on property access. The change needs an audit (and ideally a type-level guarantee) that all importers of `@calcom/app-store` await the values.

async forEach makes calendar/video deletions fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch

Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the loop was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` to await the now-async `getCalendar`, but forEach does not await async callbacks. The booking is already marked CANCELLED and the reschedule email is sent before the calendar/video event deletions complete, and any failure to delete is an unhandled rejection invisible to the surrounding try/catch. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` with individual error handling.

requestReschedule no longer awaits calendar/video deletions

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` was introduced because `getCalendar` became async. Since forEach doesn't await its callbacks, the mutation sends the reschedule email, fires webhooks, and returns while the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls are still pending; a serverless function may be frozen before they finish, leaving stale events on users' calendars, and any errors become unhandled rejections. Await the deletions with `Promise.all(...map(...))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check uses the same value for slot start and end, ignoring event length

In the new working-hours guard inside checkIfIsAvailable, both `start` and `end` are computed identically as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. The `end` should be the slot's end time (start + eventLength). As written, a slot that starts inside working hours but ends past the working-hours end (e.g. a 60-min slot starting 30 min before the end of availability) is treated as within working hours, so the fixed-host filter will not remove it — exactly the kind of over-booking this PR is trying to prevent.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object identity comparison of two dayjs objects is always false

In checkIfIsAvailable, the branch `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances with `===`, which is always false. This check was presumably meant to detect a full-day blocked override (start equal to end), but it can never trigger, so that case silently falls through to the subsequent isBefore/isSame/isAfter checks. Use `.isSame()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Override start/end minute computation wraps across midnight instead of producing out-of-range minutes

The new override mapping computes `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Because `.hour()` wraps into 0-23, an override whose adjusted time crosses midnight (e.g. organizer override 22:00-23:00 with invitee offset +3h becomes 25:00, reported as 1:00) produces a startTime/endTime in the wrong part of the day rather than minutes > 1440 or < 0 that the range logic could handle or clip. Overrides near midnight for invitees in distant timezones will show slots at completely wrong times. Compute total minutes from the shifted time (e.g. diff against start of day) instead of hour()/minute().

Slot time compared in UTC against working hours defined in organizer's timezone

`slotStartTime` is `time.utc()`, and the new check computes `slotStartTime.hour()`/`.day()` in UTC, then compares them against `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime`, which are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's (schedule) timezone. For any organizer not on UTC the comparison is shifted by their offset (e.g. an IST host's 9:30 start becomes 570, but a 9:30 IST slot is hour 4 in UTC), so slots will be incorrectly rejected or accepted for fixed hosts depending on timezone. The slot time should be converted to the organizer's timezone (organizerTimeZone is already passed in) before extracting hour/day.

dateOverrideExist flag makes a slot available whenever any override matches its day, even if slot is outside all overrides

When `dateOverrides.find(...)` runs, the callback returns true only for slots outside the matching override, which correctly leads to `return false`. But if the slot's day matches an override and none of the 'outside' conditions trigger, the find returns undefined and execution falls to `if (dateOverrideExist) return true` — bypassing the busy-time check entirely. A fixed host with a date override on that day who also has a conflicting booking or calendar busy time during the override window will be reported available, allowing double bookings. The busy check should still run for slots inside an override.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when Integration metadata lacks 'sender'

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the re-install path does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. `sender` is only stored in metadata when it is present in pipeline state (`build_integration` only adds it `if state.get("sender")`), and Integrations created before sender tracking existed (or where the installation webhook was missed) will not have a `sender` key in metadata at all. For any such pre-existing Integration that has no OrganizationIntegration (the exact path this new check runs on: 'OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist'), this raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the failure dialog. Use a guarded lookup (e.g. `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`) and treat a missing sender as a verification failure rather than crashing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
No test for the state-signature mismatch path

The PR description states the pipeline now fails 'If there is a mismatch between state parameter supplied by user and pipeline signature', which is a core security property of this change (CSRF protection on the OAuth callback). The added tests cover the user-mismatch and installation-not-found cases, but no test exercises `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` with a wrong/absent-but-present `state` value to assert the failure page is rendered and the flow aborts. A regression removing or weakening the signature check would not be caught by the test suite.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Default value timezone.now() is evaluated once at import time

The dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` a single time when the class is defined at module import, so every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` value gets the same stale timestamp (the process import time) rather than the time the source was created. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to get a per-instance timestamp.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
datetime in AssignmentSource.to_dict() will fail Celery JSON serialization

sync_group_assignee_outbound passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` (which includes the `queued` datetime) as the `assignment_source_dict` kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Sentry's Celery tasks are serialized with JSON, and a raw datetime is not JSON-serializable, so enqueueing the task will raise a serialization error (or kombu EncodeError) whenever an assignment originated from an inbound integration webhook — the exact path this PR adds. The datetime should be serialized to an ISO string (and parsed back in from_dict) or the field omitted from the task payload.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
should_sync is now always called with a second positional argument; existing overrides with the old signature will raise TypeError

The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`. Only the base classes in this PR were updated to accept the new parameter; any concrete integration installation that overrides `should_sync(self, attribute)` (a common pattern for Jira/VSTS/Azure DevOps-style integrations) will raise `TypeError: should_sync() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`, and since the task retries on unexpected exceptions, this will burn retries on every assignee sync for those providers. Callers should pass the source as a keyword and overrides need to be audited/updated, or the call should be made defensively.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses abstract StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing its abstract methods

MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed from DetectorHandler (where it implemented evaluate) to StatefulDetectorHandler with just `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data, none of which are implemented here. Because it inherits from abc.ABC, any attempt to instantiate it (e.g., via Detector.detector_handler for a detector of type metric_alert_fire) will raise TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class. Previously it was instantiable and returned an empty result list. Either implement the abstract methods (even as stubs) or keep the class on the non-abstract base until the stateful abstraction is built.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

The docstring on StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate reads 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.' but the method now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]. This contradicts the signature change made in this PR and will mislead implementers of new detector handlers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process is always False for spawn processes, so hung/dead flusher processes are never killed

The flusher explicitly creates processes with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn"), so the objects are SpawnProcess instances. However, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the *default* context's class (ForkProcess on Linux), and SpawnProcess does not subclass it. Therefore `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` (line 254) and in `join` (line 346) evaluates to False for every flusher process, and `process.kill()` / `process.terminate()` are silently never executed. Consequences: when a flusher process hangs, `_ensure_processes_alive` spawns a replacement without killing the hung one, leaving two processes flushing the same shards and producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic; and on shutdown, processes are never terminated and linger as (daemon) zombies until interpreter exit. The old single-process code had the same latent isinstance bug in `join`, but the new restart path makes it load-bearing. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or just call kill/terminate unconditionally, or track which entries are threads vs processes).

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of the process-wait loop on deadline, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes

In `join`, if the deadline is exhausted while waiting for one process, the `break` exits the for-loop over `self.processes` entirely, so none of the remaining processes get `process.terminate()` called (the terminate happens per-iteration after the wait). Previously there was only one process so this couldn't happen. With multiple flusher processes, a slow-to-stop process causes all later processes to be left running after join returns. The terminate should be applied to every remaining process even after the deadline, or the loop should continue with zero remaining time so terminate still runs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Default --flusher-processes=1 contradicts the stated goal of one flusher process per shard

The new CLI option defaults to 1, meaning a default deployment of process-spans gets a single flusher process shared across all shards via `flusher_processes` being passed to SpanFlusher. But the PR description says the intent is to "spawn a process per redis shard", and SpanFlusher's own default when max_processes is None is `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (one process per shard). Because the click default (1) is always passed, the SpanFlusher default is effectively unreachable from the CLI. If per-shard processes are the intended default, the click default should be None (or omitted) so SpanFlusher falls back to one process per shard.

Restart limit check allows MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS + 1 restarts per process

`if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` is checked before incrementing, so the RuntimeError only fires on the 12th unhealthy detection (restarts 0..10 are permitted, i.e. 11 restarts) even though the constant is named MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10. This was inherited from the previous single-process code but is now duplicated per process; with N processes the consumer tolerates 11*N restarts before crashing. Use `>=` to match the constant's intent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
No handling of partition revocation; stale offsets keep being committed after rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a background commit thread that commits whatever OffsetTracker considers committable, but nothing in the strategy or in ResultsStrategyFactory resets state when partitions are revoked during a rebalance. After a rebalance the OffsetTracker still holds entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, and the commit thread will happily commit those offsets to the consumer group, potentially clobbering progress made by the new owner of the partition. Additionally, if the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for a new assignment, a second commit thread is spawned while the old pool/tracker state lingers. Partition revocation should clear tracker state for revoked partitions and stop committing them.

Worker commits offsets for messages whose processing raised an exception

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the broad `except Exception` only logs, and the `finally` block unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset(). That means a work item whose result_processor raised is marked complete and its offset becomes committable, so the message is silently dropped rather than redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Today ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows its own exceptions so this path is rarely hit, but any exception thrown outside that wrapper (e.g. in sentry_sdk transaction handling or a future processor) causes permanent message loss with only a log line. Failed items should either not complete the offset (forcing redelivery) or be routed to the DLQ.

Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but an unbounded queue never blocks the consumer's submit path, so the Kafka consumer thread will keep polling and enqueueing WorkItems (each holding the full decoded result and original message) as fast as it can read them. If one group/queue is slow (the exact problem this PR is meant to mitigate), items pile up in memory instead of applying backpressure via the consumer, risking OOM of the consumer pod and defeating offset-based flow control. The queues should have a bounded maxsize so submit() blocks and arroyo stops polling.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is flaky and its assertion contradicts the implementation

The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call, then asserts no offsets were committed. But OrderedQueueWorker completes offsets in a finally block even when processing raises, so offset 100 becomes committable immediately and the 1-second commit loop will commit offset 101/102 for the partition. The test only passes because it breaks out of the wait loop after ~0.2s, racing the commit thread's 1.0s interval — under load or on a slow CI runner the commit can land before the assertion, making the test fail nondeterministically. Either the implementation should not commit failed offsets, or the test should assert the actual (committed-past-failure) behavior deterministically.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is checked before the permission-allow cache, so a stale denial overrides a fresh allow

In Check, the permDenialCache lookup (line 117) runs before consulting permCache via getCachedIdentityPermissions. A denial entry is written whenever a fresh DB lookup denies (line 154) and lives for shortCacheTTL (30s). If a user is denied, then granted permission, and the permission cache is subsequently refreshed with the new allowing permissions (e.g. by a concurrent Check for another resource of the same action that falls through to getUserPermissions and repopulates permCache), a later Check for the originally denied resource still hits the stale denial entry first and returns Allowed=false without ever looking at the now-correct permCache. Given the stated goal of this PR is to let creators access newly created resources quickly, the allow check should take precedence over the denial cache (or the denial entry should be invalidated when fresh permissions are stored), otherwise users can be denied for up to 30s despite correct permissions being cached.

Test case 'should return error if store fails' never triggers a store error and asserts NoError

In TestService_getUserPermissions, the case named 'should return error if store fails' sets permissions to nil but never sets err: true on the fakeStore, and the test body unconditionally calls require.NoError(t, err). The test therefore exercises a successful empty-permissions lookup, not a store failure, so the error path of getIdentityPermissions is untested and the test name is misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in the filtered results list

In the `origin === 'grafana'` branch the returned `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` no longer receives `key={key}` (the previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` had it). These elements are siblings of keyed `<DataSourceRuleLoader key={key}>` items inside the same `<ul>`, so React will warn about missing keys and, more importantly, reconciliation across pages of infinite-scroll results can reuse the wrong component instance for a different rule, showing stale state. Add `key={key}` to the `GrafanaRuleListItem` element.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item shown in list view but clicking it does nothing (drawer requires rulerRule)

`AlertRuleMenu` will show 'Silence notifications' in the list view because the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` grants the Silence ability from the prom rule. Clicking it calls `handleSilence` which sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true — and `rule` (the ruler rule) is always undefined in the list view since this PR removes ruler requests there. false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item can never appear for Grafana rules in the list view (rulerRule is always undefined there)

The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the alert list view the whole point of this PR is that no ruler API calls are made, so `RuleActionsButtons.V2` is rendered with only `promRule` and `rule` (rulerRule) is `undefined`. Even though the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` path can set `canDelete` to true from prom-rule/folder permissions, the `rulerRule &&` guard means the Delete item is never rendered in the list view, so users can no longer delete Grafana-managed rules from the list. The pause menu item at line 123 has the same problem: `canPause` can be true via the grafana ability, but rendering requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, which is false when only a promRule exists. Either the menu items need to work off the promRule (e.g. construct the delete/pause payloads from the prom rule), or the abilities should not report these actions as available.

ModifyExport ability for prom rules excludes recording rules, unlike the ruler-rule path

In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport` is `[isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]` where `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`. The equivalent ruler-based hook uses `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which matches both alerting and recording Grafana rules. So a Grafana-managed recording rule shows the Export menu in the details view (ruler path) but not in the list view (prom path). If export of recording rules is intended to remain available, use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` here; otherwise the two paths should be made consistent.

Removed coverage for creating/deleting rule states with no replacement

The PR deletes the tests 'should render rule with url and creating state when only ruler rule exists', 'should render delete rule operation list item when only prom rule exists', and the entire `matchRules` describe block, and the component no longer has any creating/deleting handling. The behavior change (a just-created rule now simply doesn't appear until Prometheus catches up, and a deleting rule renders fully actionable until it disappears) is a real UX regression risk that is now completely untested — there is no test asserting what the list shows during these eventual-consistency windows.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Template variables are now applied twice in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() before delegating to splitQueriesByStreamShard(), but each shard group is then executed via runSplitQuery() (line 163), which after this PR also calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every target again. So in the sharded path every query is interpolated at least twice (once here, and once per shard group inside runSplitQuery — the updated test even asserts applyTemplateVariables was called 5 times for a single query). Beyond the wasted work, double interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent: if a variable's value itself contains a '$'-prefixed token (e.g. a label value like '$foo'), the second pass inside runSplitQuery will re-interpolate it and corrupt the query sent to Loki. Either the interpolation here or in runSplitQuery should be skipped when the queries were already interpolated.

applyTemplateVariables invoked per shard group via runSplitQuery

Because runSplitQuery now unconditionally calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on all targets, the shard-splitting flow (which pre-interpolates in runShardSplitQuery and then calls runSplitQuery once per shard group) re-runs template variable interpolation on every shard sub-request, even though the expressions are already fully interpolated and only differ by the injected __stream_shard__ selector. For dashboards with many template variables this repeats the interpolation/scopedVar resolution work for every shard group; consider interpolating once and passing the results through.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID is no longer included in the "Plugin Request Completed" log entry

Before this change, LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly appended "traceID" (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params, along with pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName and dsUID. Now those fields are only present if the incoming context carries the contextual attributes added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware — but that middleware never adds a traceID, and the tracing import was removed from this file. Unless pkg/infra/log's ConcreteLogger.FromContext injects traceID automatically (which the old explicit code suggests it does not), the traceID field silently disappears from the egress log line, breaking log-to-trace correlation for anyone relying on the traceID field of this event.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh instance, so logs are not recorded

TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a brand-new instance, rather than the receiver. All other TestLogger methods record calls into f.DebugLogs/InfoLogs/etc., which tests then assert on. With this change, LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that constructs a TestLogger, passes it to NewLoggerMiddleware, and then inspects InfoLogs will always see zero calls and an empty message — the log entry is recorded on a throwaway logger. The fake should return the receiver itself (f) so recorded logs remain observable, matching how a contextual logger is expected to behave.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Contextual log fields now silently depend on middleware ordering

LoggerMiddleware no longer sets pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, or uname itself; it relies on ContextualLoggerMiddleware having already enriched the context via FromContext(ctx). In pluginsintegration.go the ordering is correct (ContextualLoggerMiddleware before LoggerMiddleware), but nothing in the code enforces or documents this dependency — if the LoggerMiddleware is ever used without the ContextualLoggerMiddleware ahead of it (or the order is swapped), the "Plugin Request Completed" log will silently lose all plugin-identifying fields. A comment on logRequest or NewLoggerMiddleware documenting this requirement would prevent a subtle observability regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is racy: count-then-insert is not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then conditionally inserting. Two (or more) concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. On a busy instance with many simultaneous first-time anonymous visitors, the limit can be breached by an arbitrary margin. Enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g., insert guarded by a transaction with a locked count, a UNIQUE/sequence-based cap, or accepting the race and documenting it).

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ErrDeviceLimitReached aborts anonymous authentication with a raw internal error

TagDevice is now called synchronously in Authenticate, and ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned as the authenticate error. The authn framework will treat this as a failed authentication, so every request from a new anonymous device (once the limit is hit) fails with an unhandled internal error rather than a controlled response (e.g., a 429 or a rendered 'device limit reached' page). The error message 'device limit reached' is also a bare fmt.Errorf with no user-facing wording, and browsers will keep retrying, generating error noise. The authn error handling for this case (status code, redirect behavior, user message) should be explicitly implemented and tested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Known device older than 30 days is rejected as 'device limit reached'

When the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within [now-30d, now+1m] and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when 0 rows are affected. The cleanup job (DeleteDevicesOlderThan) only deletes devices older than 61 days, so a device whose last update is between 30 and 61 days old still occupies a row (and is counted by CountDevices) but cannot be updated — its owner gets a hard 'device limit reached' auth error even though refreshing that existing device would not increase the device count. The update branch should fall back to checking whether the device row exists (and update it) before concluding the limit blocks the request.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the store write, so a rejected/failed tag is not retried for 29 minutes

tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails (including ErrDeviceLimitReached or a transient DB error), the cache entry remains and subsequent requests from the same device skip the store entirely for up to 29 minutes. With the new synchronous error path this means a transient DB failure during the limit check or insert silently stops device tracking, and TagDevice returns an error to the caller on the first attempt but nil on subsequent ones, giving inconsistent auth behavior. Only populate the cache after a successful store call, or evict on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Extra COUNT query on every device tag when a limit is configured

When deviceLimit > 0, every CreateOrUpdateDevice call performs a full COUNT(*) over anon_device filtered by updated_at before deciding whether to insert. For known devices this count is wasted work (the upsert would have succeeded anyway), and without an index on updated_at this is a table scan per new/refreshing device. Consider only doing the count when the upsert would create a new row, or checking existence of the device_id first.

New device_limit option is not added to sample config or docs

The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit setting is parsed but is not added to conf/sample.ini (or defaults.ini comments), so administrators have no discoverable documentation of the option, its default (0 = unlimited), or its semantics (limit over a rolling 30-day window). The PR description also leaves the docs checkbox unchecked.

anonymousDeviceLimit is always serialized and typed inconsistently with the frontend

The Go DTO field AnonymousDeviceLimit is a plain int64 with no omitempty, so the JSON payload always contains "anonymousDeviceLimit": 0 even when no limit is configured, while the TypeScript type in packages/grafana-data declares it as `number | undefined`. Consumers cannot distinguish 'no limit configured' from 'limit of 0' except by the 0-as-unset convention, which is undocumented. Either make it a pointer/omitempty or type the frontend field as a plain number and document the 0 = unlimited convention.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup routine logs normal operation at Error level, including full ID lists

The new cleanup code logs every batch at Error level: `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...)` (line 534), `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...)` (line 537), and the equivalents for count-based cleanup (lines 554, 557) and orphaned tag cleanup (lines 576, 579). These are not errors — they fire on every successful batch of a job that runs on a schedule, and they include the full `ids` slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries per line). This will flood error-level logs, trigger log-based alerting on errors that aren't errors, and produce very large log lines. They should be Debug level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all cleanup jobs

This PR changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This does not just make annotation cleanup run more often — it makes every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, temp user invites, short URLs, query history, tmp file deletion) run 10x more frequently. Several of these do non-trivial database deletes and filesystem scans, and query history cleanup enforces row limits over large tables. This is an undocumented, broad behavioral/performance change bundled into a PR about avoiding annotation deadlocks; if the intent was only to make annotation cleanup more responsive, the annotation job should get its own schedule rather than speeding up the entire cleanup loop.

false_positives.candidate:
MaxCount cleanup can exit early if a fetched batch is concurrently deleted

In the new split fetch-then-delete flow, `untilDoneOrCancelled` stops when a batch reports zero affected rows. Because the SELECT and DELETE are no longer in one statement/transaction, another process (e.g., a second Grafana instance's cleanup job, or a user delete) can delete the fetched IDs between the two statements, making `RowsAffected()` return 0 and terminating the loop even though more annotations beyond MaxCount still exist. The old single-statement form re-evaluated the subquery on each execution and only stopped when a delete genuinely matched nothing. The under-deleted rows will be cleaned on the next cycle so the impact is bounded, but it is a behavioral regression worth noting/acknowledging (e.g., loop while len(ids) == batchSize instead of affected > 0).

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete installs the wrong logger into the context

Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then calls `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` with the base logger instead of `log`. All log lines emitted from within the storage/legacy delete calls (and the `log.Error` in this function uses `log`, but anything retrieved via klog.FromContext downstream) lose the name/kind/method values that the other methods attach.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the metric 'kind' label

On the success path of Delete, the metric is recorded as `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object name where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. This creates a high-cardinality metric label (one series per deleted object name) and breaks aggregation by kind for delete operations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the (soon-to-be-cancelled) request context

In Create (and identically in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection), the legacy write is launched in a goroutine that derives its context from the incoming request `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)`. When Create returns to the caller, the API server completes the HTTP request and cancels the request context, which immediately cancels the goroutine's context as well. The 'safe measure' legacy write will therefore usually fail with context canceled before it even runs, so in mode 3 the legacy store will silently drift out of sync with unified storage. The goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`) while keeping only the values (logger, auth info) needed. This affects lines 51, 110, 135, and 163.

DeleteCollection async legacy call recorded with the storage metric

Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection latency/errors will be attributed to unified storage, and the actual storage call was already recorded above, so every delete-collection produces two storage-metric samples and no legacy-metric sample.

Storage failures recorded with the legacy-duration metric

In Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — recording a legacy error/duration even though the legacy store was never called. The same mistake exists in Update at line 129 (`recordLegacyDuration` on a `d.Storage.Update` failure). This corrupts the dual-writer metrics: legacy error rates and latencies will show failures that actually belong to unified storage, misleading anyone alerting on these metrics during the migration.

Tests don't verify the async legacy write happens

The mode 3 write-path tests set up legacy mock expectations but then never wait for the goroutine or assert the legacy call occurred (e.g. TestMode3_Create's error case doesn't even set up a storage mock failing — the 'unified store fails' case configures only the legacy mock to fail, while the actual storage mock has no expectation, so `dw.Create` panics/fails on an unexpected call rather than exercising the intended path, and no test asserts `ls` was eventually called). As written, the tests pass even if the legacy write is dropped entirely (e.g. due to the cancelled-context bug), so they don't protect the core guarantee of mode 3.

Update passes the same UpdatedObjectInfo to both stores, losing the pre-computed updated object

The previous implementation of mode 3 Update first did `Storage.Get`, called `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` once, and then wrapped the result in an `updateWrapper` so both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update received a wrapper returning the already-computed object. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Storage.Update` and then to `d.Legacy.Update` in the async goroutine. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations used by the API machinery generally wrap the request body and may only be consumed once (e.g. they decode the incoming object on each call, or hold the old object fetched by the first Update call). The second invocation in the legacy goroutine can fail or produce an object computed against a different 'old' state than unified storage used, so legacy can store content that differs from what was written to unified storage — the opposite of what the dual write is meant to guarantee.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions ignores the sqlExpressions feature flag entirely

The new enableSqlExpressions() unconditionally returns false: it computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every path, so even operators who explicitly enable the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle will get the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented" for every SQL expression query. If hard-disabling is the intent of this security fix, the convoluted always-false logic is misleading — a plain `return false` (or removing the feature flag check and the flag reference) would be honest about the behavior. As written, the feature flag documentation (which this PR explicitly says it is leaving untouched) tells users a toggle exists that silently does nothing, and the dead negation invites a future edit to mistakenly re-enable the vulnerable code path by 'fixing' what looks like a bug.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which serialized builds. Now the lock is only taken when inserting into the cache, and getOrCreateIndex in search.go has no per-key locking (its own TODO acknowledges this). Two concurrent requests (or a request plus a watch event) for the same NamespacedResource can both see GetIndex return nil, both run a full bleve build, and both assign b.cache[key] — the loser's index is never closed (file handles/disk for file-backed indexes leak) and duplicate work is done. A per-key build mutex or singleflight is needed to keep the finer-grained locking safe.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes b.cache[key] under cacheMu at line 138 and GetIndex reads under RLock. Previously BuildIndex held cacheMu for its whole duration, so writes only happened while no other BuildIndex was running, but TotalDocs was still unsafe — and this PR makes it worse by calling TotalDocs from searchSupport.init's new log line and by allowing concurrent builds. A concurrent map read and write panics at runtime. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() while iterating.

false_positives.candidate:
Data races on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed inside errgroup goroutines

In searchSupport.init, each goroutine spawned by group.Go writes to the outer shared variables: `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190). These run concurrently with up to initWorkers goroutines and with the main goroutine which reads/overwrites `err` at `err = group.Wait()`. This is an unsynchronized read/write race (flagged by -race) on both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`, and the span attribute count can be undercounted. Use an atomic counter (or collect per-goroutine) and return the build error only via the goroutine's return value instead of assigning to the shared err.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the cancelable context

NewResourceServer creates ctx/cancel, then calls s.Init(ctx) and returns nil, err on failure without calling cancel(). The background context and its goroutine resources are never released on the error path. Call cancel() before returning the error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDP

In testCacheIDPForLogin, the loop that creates 20 IDPs registers cleanup with getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) — the string "alias" is a literal, not the loop variable alias ("idp-alias-" + i). The same mistake is repeated at line 425 for "idp-alias-20". As a result the cleanup removes a non-existent IDP named "alias" and the 20+ created identity providers leak into subsequent tests in the class (e.g. testCacheIDPByOrg counts IDPs and can see these leftover brokers), making tests order-dependent and flaky.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login IDP cache is not invalidated when an organization is removed or disabled

getForLogin caches IDP id sets per (FetchMode, organizationId), but unlike getByOrganization it never checks isInvalid(orgId), and no invalidation of the cacheKeyForLogin keys is registered when an organization is removed, disabled, or when an IDP is linked/unlinked through the organization API without going through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update() (the invalidation in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate only fires on the update() path and relies on the caller passing an updated model with the new organizationId). If an org is deleted or its broker link is changed outside update(), the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL login lists keep returning the old IDP ids, so the login page can show brokers for a removed/disabled organization until the entry is evicted. getByOrganization handles this exact case with the isInvalid(orgId) check; getForLogin should do the same (or org removal/unlink should register invalidation for all login cache keys).

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an arbitrary JRE provider, not BouncyCastle

AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the JVM default keystore (typically the SUN provider). Callers of CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() reasonably expect a BouncyCastle(-like) provider and pass it to JCE getInstance(..., provider) calls for BC-specific algorithms; with this implementation they will get NoSuchAlgorithmException or silently use a provider that lacks the expected algorithms. If this provider is selected (it wins whenever no other CryptoProvider jar is present, which is exactly the standalone authz-client scenario), any code path touching getBouncyCastleProvider() misbehaves instead of failing clearly. Returning null or throwing UnsupportedOperationException like the other unsupported methods would be safer.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: two ASN1Encoder results discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances and call write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) on them, but the results are thrown away; the actual encoding is redone in the return statement with fresh encoders. This dead code is confusing and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence() silently accepts indefinite-length encoding and returns incomplete data

ASN1Decoder.readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80), and readSequence() uses `while (length > 0)`, so an indefinite-length SEQUENCE is silently parsed as an empty sequence instead of being rejected. The caller in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS then throws only a misleading 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2'. Since the decoder is only meant to handle DER (which forbids indefinite lengths), readSequence should throw an IOException when readLength() returns -1 to fail loudly on malformed input.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all external CryptoProvider implementations

The PR adds `int order();` as an abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (the interface is explicitly designed for pluggable crypto integrations, e.g. custom FIPS providers) will now fail to compile or throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when the new CryptoIntegration sorting calls order(). Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 100; }`) would preserve compatibility while still allowing the built-in providers to override it.

false_positives.candidate:
Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only asserts round-trip

ECDSAAlgorithmTest generates a single default-curve (P-256) EC key pair in the constructor and reuses it for testES384 and testES512, so the signatures being converted were produced by a curve that doesn't match those algorithms' real key sizes. Additionally the test only asserts that derToRS(rsToDer(x)) == x; it never verifies the produced DER against a Signature.verify() or a known-good JWS vector, so a systematically wrong encoding that round-trips would go undetected. Verifying the re-encoded DER with java.security.Signature (initialized with the matching curve key) would make the test meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client resource lookup uses resource server id as owner while resources are created with client id as owner

`hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` looks up the per-client resource via `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())`, i.e. with owner = `server.getId()`. However `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` creates these resources with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())`, i.e. owner = the client's id (`resourceServer.getClientId()`), which is a different value from the resource server's id. If the store filters by owner when a non-null owner is passed, the per-client resource created for a specific Clients permission will never be found here, so evaluation silently falls back to the all-clients resource and per-client grants/denies (e.g. a negative permission on one client) are ignored. Either pass `null`/the same owner used at creation time, or make creation and lookup consistent.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible null resource dereferenced in findByResource for all-clients fallback

When no per-client resource exists, the code does `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE);` and immediately calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. `getResourceTypeResource()` can return `null` (it returns null when the resource store has no resource named 'Clients', e.g. for a resource server created before this schema type existed or after a failed init), so `findByResource(server, null)` will throw an NPE instead of simply denying permission. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

The event listener now wraps cleanup in `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` and calls `management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)` on `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent`. When the v2 feature (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) is also enabled, `AdminPermissions.management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2`, whose `clients()` now returns the new `ClientPermissionsV2`, and `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled()` unconditionally throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. Because this runs inside a ProviderEventListener during client deletion, deleting any client in such a deployment will blow up with an UnsupportedOperationException (or leave the deletion inconsistent). Javadoc for requireView()/requireViewClientScopes() describes return values for void methods

The newly added Javadoc for `requireView()` says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}" and `requireViewClientScopes()` similarly says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}", but both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException on failure. The documentation is copy-pasted from the boolean accessors and misstates the contract; it should say it throws ForbiddenException if the corresponding can* method returns false, as done for the other require* methods.

getResourceName not extended for the new Clients resource type

`getResourceName()` only special-cases the Users resource type. For the newly added Clients type, per-client resources are stored with the client's UUID as the resource name (see `resolveClient` returning `client.getId()`), but the method falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is typically null for these programmatically created resources. Any UI/API that renders permission resource names (e.g. the admin console permission list) will show nothing or a raw UUID instead of the client's clientId. Add a Clients branch resolving the client and returning its clientId, mirroring the Users branch.

canManage() grants manage access to admins holding only the view scope

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set. The returned set is consumed by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource as `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute and passed to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`, where the values must be group IDs used to filter users by group membership. In the V2 schema the group ID is stored as the resource *name* (AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup returns group.getId() as the resource name), while resource.getId() is the internal UUID of the authorization resource. As a result, admins who should see users through group view-members/manage-members permissions will get empty user lists and zero counts because the membership filter uses non-existent group IDs. Possible null resource passed to policyStore.findByResource when all-groups resource is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Locale-stripping regex character class also matches [ \\ ] ^ _

The pattern `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties` uses the character class `[a-zA-Z-_]`, where `Z-_` is a range that also includes the characters `[`, `\`, `]`, `^`, and `_`. On Windows, absolute paths contain `\` separators, so the greedy `*` can match across directory boundaries and produce a wrong English file path (e.g. consuming a backslash and parts of parent directories when a path segment contains an underscore followed by `.properties`). It would be safer to use an explicit class like `[a-zA-Z_-]` or to derive the English file name from the file name only rather than from the whole absolute path.

Missing English reference file crashes the build with an unhelpful RuntimeException

`verifySafeHtml()` computes the English counterpart path and opens it unconditionally; if it does not exist (e.g. a new translated properties file is added before its `_en` counterpart, or the path mapping above mis-resolves), a plain `RuntimeException("unable to read file ...")` is thrown instead of a `MojoExecutionException`. Unlike `verify()`, which wraps IO errors into `MojoExecutionException`, this escapes the mojo's error handling and aborts the build with a raw stack trace instead of a clean verification error message. The same applies to the target bundle read at line 67.

error-invalid-multivalued-size switched to {0}/{choice} syntax in a JS bundle that uses {{ }} interpolation

All other messages in the admin-ui and account-ui property files use the i18next `{{0}}` placeholder syntax (e.g. `'{{0}}' must have maximal value of {{2}}.`). This change rewrites `error-invalid-multivalued-size` to Java MessageFormat syntax (`{0}`, `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`). If the React apps render this message via i18next, the placeholders and the choice expression will not be interpolated and users will see the literal raw string, including the `{2,choice,...}` expression. The same change was applied to `js/apps/account-ui/.../messages_en.properties` (line 188). Unless the JS apps have explicitly added MessageFormat support for this key, the server-style choice format belongs only in the Java theme bundles under `themes/`, not in the JS bundles.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted grant check and wrong substring offsets

The new isAccessTokenId matcher is broken in two ways. First, the grant shortcut is at characters 4-5 of the 6-char prefix (e.g. "onrtac" -> "ac"), but the code uses items[0].substring(3, 5), which yields "ta" and never equals any grant shortcut. Second, the condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) when the shortcut *does* equal the expected one. The combined effect is that the matcher accepts any token ID regardless of grant type (since the substring never matches, the inverted check never triggers), so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectAuthReqIdToToken/expectDeviceCodeToToken no longer actually verify the encoded grant type. If someone later fixes only the offset, the inverted condition would make all these tests fail. The check should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.
