false_positives.candidate:
Token exchange sets GRANT_TYPE attribute after access token may already be built in other exchange paths

In StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient, `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.TOKEN_EXCHANGE_GRANT_TYPE)` is set only here; however the TokenManager.initToken that encodes the grant type into the token ID runs inside responseBuilder.generateAccessToken(), which is fine for this path. But other token-exchange providers (e.g. AbstractTokenExchangeProvider subclasses such as the legacy/standard V1 exchange and subject-impersonation flows) also generate access tokens via the TokenManager without setting Constants.GRANT_TYPE on the client session context, so their tokens will be encoded with grant "na" instead of "te". Given the PR's stated goal (token-exchange use case #37117 relying on the grant type in the token ID), tokens issued by those exchange paths will carry the wrong/unknown grant. Also note the import of TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory added in this file is unused.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Used recovery codes in user storage are never consumed, allowing replay

createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the raw generated codes (JSON-serialized plaintext list) in the user storage via UserCredentialModel. Unlike the local keycloak-recovery-authn-codes provider, whose isValid() marks a code as used and persists the updated credential, a federated user storage only validates the presented code against the stored list (see BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid, which does anyMatch without removing anything). Because no updated credential is written back after a successful authentication, a recovery code stored in user storage remains valid forever and can be reused by anyone who has seen it, defeating the one-time-use semantics of recovery codes. Additionally, the codes are transmitted to and held by the user storage as plaintext rather than the hashed form used in local storage, which weakens the at-rest protection for federated stores.

removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete federated recovery-code credentials

The lookup was changed to RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which now also returns credentials from federated user storage (getFederatedCredentialsStream). However, when all codes are used the code still calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...), which only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage. For a user whose recovery codes live in a federated user storage, the removal silently does nothing: the 'all codes used' credential persists in the user storage, and every subsequent login will keep re-adding the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action while the stale credential remains. The deletion path needs to handle federated credentials (e.g., via disableCredentialType/updateCredential on the user storage) or skip removal when the credential is federated.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount now silently returns null on concurrent deletion instead of failing fast

With this change, getSubGroupsCount returns null when the underlying group has been concurrently deleted. Every other accessor in GroupAdapter that encounters a missing delegate either falls back to cached data or throws IllegalStateException("Not found in database") (see getDelegateForUpdate/isUpdated), while getRoleMappingsStream/getSubGroupsStream detect staleness and delegate to the DB. Returning a null Long here is inconsistent and will surface as a silently missing subGroupCount in GroupRepresentation (populated via GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount), which callers may not distinguish from a genuinely unknown count, and could NPE any code that auto-unboxes the result. Consider aligning the behavior with the rest of the adapter (throw or delegate) rather than returning null.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined before asserting on caughtExceptions, making the test racy and leaky

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, after deletedAll.set(true) the test immediately asserts assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty()) without joining the reader thread. The reader thread may still be in the middle of a groups() request when deletedAll flips, so an NPE thrown by that in-flight request is added to caughtExceptions after the assertion has already passed — the very race this test is meant to catch can be missed, and the test can pass while the bug still reproduces. The thread should be joined before asserting.

This contradicts the strategy docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Today ResultProcessor.__call__ swallows its own exceptions so this path is rarely hit, but any exception thrown outside that wrapper (e.g. in sentry_sdk transaction handling or a future processor) causes permanent message loss with only a log line. Additionally, if the factory's create_with_partitions is called again for a new assignment, a second commit thread is spawned while the old pool/tracker state lingers. The test only passes because it breaks out of the wait loop after ~0.2s, racing the commit thread's 1.0s interval — under load or on a slow CI runner the commit can land before the assertion, making the test fail nondeterministically. Either the implementation should not commit failed offsets, or the test should assert the actual (committed-past-failure) behavior deterministically.

`URI(website.to_s).host rescue nil` returns nil for values like `example.com/user` (no scheme — URI parses it as a path, host is nil) or any malformed URL that survives profile validation, causing `website_name` to be nil and the template's `{{#if model.website_name}}` to hide the website link entirely even though `model.website` is present. Previously the client-side code displayed `website.split('/')[2]`, which also degraded, but the new serializer should fall back to the raw `website` string instead of returning nil so the link remains visible.

Query string and fragment are dropped from displayed website name

When the domains match, the display value is built as `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path`, discarding any query string or fragment. A user whose website is `http://example.com/page?id=5` on the same host will see it displayed as `example.com/page`, which no longer represents the actual URL. Include `URI#query`/`fragment` or use `request_uri` when constructing the display path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring match

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that merely appears as a substring of discourseUrl. An origin like `https://evil.com/redirect?https://forum.example.com` would pass if discourseUrl is configured correspondingly, and more simply the check never validates that e.origin actually equals the forum's origin. Any site able to get a message to the parent window can resize the iframe; the check should compare e.origin against a parsed expected origin.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation for postMessage relies on an insecure `indexOf` substring check instead of properly validating the exact origin, allowing it to be bypassed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content can be nil, crashing the hourly feed job

In poll_feed, `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has a `content` element. Plain RSS 2.0 feeds typically only have `description`, not `content`, so SimpleRSS will return nil and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the entire feed poll (and because `sidekiq_options retry: false`, nothing is retried and no items from that feed are imported until the next hour, which will crash the same way). Use `i.content || i.description` and guard for nil.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `i.content.scrub` can fail with a nil error because RSS feeds often lack `content`, and suggests the same solution of falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method stores and serves completely unsanitized HTML

`cook` returns `raw` verbatim when cook_method is :raw_html, so posts imported via TopicEmbed.import (feed polling or remote retrieval of the embeddable host) bypass PrettyText/Sanitize entirely and are served as-is (the embed view even does `raw post.cooked`). Any script/event-handler markup in a fetched article or feed item becomes stored XSS on the forum itself, visible in topic pages, digests, and embeds. The imported HTML should be run through Sanitize with an allowlist before storage.

Check-then-create on embed_url races and raises RecordNotUnique

import() does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and then `TopicEmbed.create!` inside a transaction. The migration adds a unique index on embed_url, so two concurrent imports of the same URL (hourly PollFeed plus a RetrieveTopic job enqueued from embed#best, which explicitly runs PollFeed and then fetches HTTP itself) will both find no row and one will crash with ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique. Rescue RecordNotUnique and fall back to the update path, or use an upsert.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

Any href/src starting with '/' is prefixed with the article's scheme+host. Protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/x.jpg` start with '/', so they are rewritten to `http://host/cdn.example.com/x.jpg`, breaking those links/images in every imported post. Check for a leading '//' and skip (or prepend only the scheme) before treating the URL as host-relative.

feed_key is dead code; job does no change detection

feed_key computes a redis key 'feed-modified:<sha>' but nothing ever reads or writes it, and poll_feed re-downloads the feed and re-hashes/re-imports every item every hour. Either wire the key up to skip unchanged feeds (e.g. via If-Modified-Since/ETag or content hash) or remove it; as-is every hourly run re-fetches all items and calls PostRevisor/sha comparisons for each.

Editing an already-shipped migration to add force: true

CreateTopTopics already ran in existing deployments; changing `create_table :top_topics` to `force: true` modifies history. Environments that haven't run it yet (or that replay migrations, e.g. some CI/staging rebuilds after a partially applied state) will silently DROP and recreate the top_topics table, losing all aggregated counts. New behavior should go in a new migration rather than editing an old one.

X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL is non-standard and unsupported

`response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = 'ALLOWALL'` is not a valid X-Frame-Options value (ALLOW-FROM requires a URI and is unsupported in Chrome/Safari; ALLOWALL is ignored entirely by most browsers). The effect is only achieved because an invalid value happens to be ignored — better to explicitly remove the header so the intent is clear and future middleware adding a default DENY doesn't break embeds.

import mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "\n<hr>..."` appends the 'imported from' footer directly to the string passed in. Callers that reuse the buffer (e.g. the Readability document content or anything comparing the original afterwards) get silently modified data, and the sha1 is computed over the mutated value. Duplicate the string (`contents = contents + ...` or `contents.dup`) before appending.

Throws if #discourse-comments element is missing

`comments.appendChild(iframe)` runs without checking that `document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` found an element. Site owners paste this snippet into arbitrary templates; if the container is absent or renamed, the script throws and no iframe is created, with no useful error. Bail out early (or log a clear message) when comments is null.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF downsize passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH

The uploads controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)`. For animated GIFs, `optimize` selects `downsize_instructions_animated`, which delegates to `resize_instructions_animated` and produces `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80% ...`. gifsicle does not accept a percentage for `--resize-fit`; the command fails, `convert_with` returns false, and the retry loop in the controller burns all 5 attempts without shrinking the file. Animated GIFs over the size limit can therefore never be uploaded, and the failure is silent (`&> /dev/null`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: passing '80%' as dimensions to gifsicle's `--resize-fit` for animated GIFs fails silently because it expects `WxH` geometry rather than a percentage.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize retry loop ignores failure and retries identical work

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > limit` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` but never checks its boolean return value. If the conversion fails (bad image, missing convert/gifsicle, unsupported format), the file size never changes and the same failing command is executed 5 times synchronously inside the deferred job before falling through to `Upload.create_for`, which will then fail validation anyway. The result is wasted CPU and a confusing generic error instead of surfacing that the image could not be processed. Break out of the loop when `downsize` returns false.

Download cap hardcoded to 10MB for API URL uploads

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. While the intent is to allow downloading larger originals for downsizing, this also caps downloads for sites whose configured image limit is above 10MB (they could previously pull larger files), and it downloads full-size originals for non-image types too, with the size magic number duplicated between the controller and the JS client. This should derive from a single setting (e.g. a multiple of max_image_size_kb) rather than a literal.

Downsizing SVGs and other vector/odd formats with `convert -resize 80%` can corrupt or balloon them

The guard uses `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`, which (matching the client-side list) includes SVG. Running ImageMagick `-resize 80%` on an SVG rasterizes it and writes the result over the original path with the `.svg` extension, producing a mislabeled raster file or a failure; repeated attempts can also grow the file, making the loop spin. SVGs (and potentially other formats that don't shrink meaningfully at 80% quality-agnostic resize) should be excluded from the auto-downsize path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TopicUser.find_by can return nil, causing a 500 on unsubscribe

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` is not guaranteed to exist. Users can receive notification emails without ever having a topic_users row for the topic (e.g. mailing-list mode subscribers, or users notified via category watching where the row was never created). In that case `tu.notification_level` on line 107 raises NoMethodError and the unsubscribe link from the email returns a 500. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` which creates the row when missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `TopicUser.find_by` can return `nil` if no record exists, and subsequently calling methods on `tu` will raise an exception/crash.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe mutates notification state on a plain GET request

The new `unsubscribe` action is exposed via GET (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"`) and immediately changes the user's `notification_level` in the database before rendering. GET requests are issued without user intent by mail-client link prefetchers, virus scanners (e.g. Outlook SafeLinks), and browser prerendering, and they carry no CSRF protection. Any such automated fetch of the unsubscribe URL will silently mute/change the user's topic subscription. Unsubscribe-via-GET should either require a POST confirmation or at minimum not apply the state change until the user confirms on the rendered page.

Direct save bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

The action mutates `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of `TopicUser.change`. As a result `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not set, and no `notification_level_change` message is published on MessageBus, so any open browser tabs of that user keep showing the old notification state and reporting that relies on the changed-at/reason fields is wrong. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` for consistency with every other code path that changes notification levels.

ensure_logged_in blocks the email unsubscribe flow for logged-out users

`unsubscribe` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` filter list. The feature's entry point is a link in a notification email, and recipients frequently are not logged in (mobile mail clients, different browser). Those users are bounced to the login page and, even after logging in, are not taken back to the unsubscribe URL, so the one-click unsubscribe silently fails for exactly the audience it targets. Consider a signed token in the unsubscribe URL (like the existing digest unsubscribe key) instead of requiring a session.

Watching/tracking users are demoted to 'regular', still receiving notifications

The logic sets the level to `regular` when it is currently above regular, and only mutes when it is regular or below. A user watching a topic (the most common reason for getting email) who clicks 'stop receiving notifications about this topic' is moved to regular, under which they still receive reply/mention notifications. The email copy ('To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here') and the page text ('You will stop receiving notifications') then claim the opposite of what happened.

unsubscribe_link now requires %{unsubscribe_url} but not all callers pass it

The `unsubscribe_link` translation now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` in `Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` is invoked for every email built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`; any current or future caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link` without passing `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. plugins, or the spec's own builder which previously only used `add_unsubscribe_link: true`) will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and the email will fail to send. Either make the per-topic sentence conditional on the URL being present or guard against the missing key.

No controller/request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The PR adds a state-changing endpoint (`topics#unsubscribe`), new routes, and a mailer link, but the only spec change is adding an `unsubscribe_url` option to an existing message-builder test. There is no coverage for the redirect-on-slug-mismatch branch, the level-downgrade/mute logic, the nil TopicUser case, or the requirement that the user be logged in — all of which contain bugs noted above.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache mutation never invalidates connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in UI

The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` callback, but unlike `disconnectMutation` right below it, it has no `onSettled` that invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. After a user deletes the cache, the `cacheUpdatedAt` value rendered in this same dropdown still comes from the old query data, so the dropdown keeps showing 'Cache Status / Last updated' and the delete option even though the cache rows were just deleted. If the parent doesn't pass an `onChanged` that refetches (it's optional), the stale state persists indefinitely. Add `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` on success/settled for the delete-cache mutation.

ENV_FILE relative path breaks depending on invocation directory

`ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's current working directory, not the script's location. Running the script from the repo root (the natural way: `./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh`) resolves to a `.env` one level above the repo and silently creates/updates the wrong file. Resolve the path from the script's own directory, e.g. `ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)/.env"`.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check uses the same value for slot start and end, ignoring event length

In the new working-hours guard inside checkIfIsAvailable, both `start` and `end` are computed identically as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. The `end` should be the slot's end time (start + eventLength). As written, a slot that starts inside working hours but ends past the working-hours end (e.g. a 60-min slot starting 30 min before the end of availability) is treated as within working hours, so the fixed-host filter will not remove it — exactly the kind of over-booking this PR is trying to prevent.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact bug described in the golden comment: the end time calculation is erroneously using `slotStartTime` instead of the slot's actual end time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object identity comparison of two dayjs objects is always false

In checkIfIsAvailable, the branch `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two distinct dayjs object instances with `===`, which is always false. This check was presumably meant to detect a full-day blocked override (start equal to end), but it can never trigger, so that case silently falls through to the subsequent isBefore/isSame/isAfter checks. Use `.isSame()` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `===` to compare two `dayjs` objects (`dayjs(date.start).add(...)` and `dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which compares object references rather than values and always evaluates to false. Both recommend using `.isSame()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Slot time compared in UTC against working hours defined in organizer's timezone

`slotStartTime` is `time.utc()`, and the new check computes `slotStartTime.hour()`/`.day()` in UTC, then compares them against `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime`, which are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's (schedule) timezone. For any organizer not on UTC the comparison is shifted by their offset (e.g. an IST host's 9:30 start becomes 570, but a 9:30 IST slot is hour 4 in UTC), so slots will be incorrectly rejected or accepted for fixed hosts depending on timezone. The slot time should be converted to the organizer's timezone (organizerTimeZone is already passed in) before extracting hour/day.

Override start/end minute computation wraps across midnight instead of producing out-of-range minutes

The new override mapping computes `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. Because `.hour()` wraps into 0-23, an override whose adjusted time crosses midnight (e.g. organizer override 22:00-23:00 with invitee offset +3h becomes 25:00, reported as 1:00) produces a startTime/endTime in the wrong part of the day rather than minutes > 1440 or < 0 that the range logic could handle or clip. Overrides near midnight for invitees in distant timezones will show slots at completely wrong times. Compute total minutes from the shifted time (e.g. diff against start of day) instead of hour()/minute().

dateOverrideExist flag makes a slot available whenever any override matches its day, even if slot is outside all overrides

When `dateOverrides.find(...)` runs, the callback returns true only for slots outside the matching override, which correctly leads to `return false`. But if the slot's day matches an override and none of the 'outside' conditions trigger, the find returns undefined and execution falls to `if (dateOverrideExist) return true` — bypassing the busy-time check entirely. A fixed host with a date override on that day who also has a conflicting booking or calendar busy time during the override window will be reported available, allowing double bookings. The busy check should still run for slots inside an override.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded retryCount update in catch block can crash the whole cron run

The catch handler now performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update` before logging. If that update itself throws (e.g., the database error that caused the original exception persists, or the row was concurrently deleted), the exception propagates out of the for-loop, the handler returns a 500, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are skipped for this run. findMany method removed, breaking existing callers

Any existing caller that invoked `service.findMany({ select: ... })` to query `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized` will now fail to compile (or at runtime), and callers must now hand-write `$queryRaw` SQL against the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table themselves, duplicating table/column knowledge outside the service. getBaseConditions integration test asserts exact result set without ORDER BY and without isolating other rows

For a collective booking with two calendar references, the block that iterates over every user credential and every updated booking is executed once per reference, so each event is deleted N times (and `apiDeletes` collects duplicates). Besides wasted API calls, some providers error on deleting an already-deleted event. Additionally, the inner loop still only deletes `updBooking.references.find(...)` — the first calendar reference per booking — so extra hosts' references are never removed. The recurring-delete block should run once outside the per-reference loop, and should iterate over all calendar references of each updated booking.

No tests cover the new multi-host destinationCalendar behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective". This change alters the `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` contract from a single object to an array and rewires create/update/delete paths across Google, Office365, Lark, CalDAV, EventManager, cancellation, rescheduling, and payment webhooks — including subtle per-credential calendar selection and booking reference persistence (`referencesToCreate` now uses `result.externalId`/`result.credentialId`). Given regressions like the empty-array crash in `EventManager.create` and the Office365 first-calendar-only behavior, at minimum unit tests for `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` with multiple hosts and for the no-destination-calendar case should be required before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach makes calendar/video deletions fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch

In `Reschedule`, the loop over `bookingRefsFiltered` was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` because `getCalendar` is now async. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, so all `calendar.deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` calls are now unawaited: the function proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns `true` before deletions finish, and any rejection inside a callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection that the surrounding `try/catch` (which only catches synchronous errors) will never see. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (optionally with per-item catch) so failures are logged and deletions complete before the email is sent.

Same issue as in vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the loop was changed to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` to await the now-async `getCalendar`, but forEach does not await async callbacks. The booking is already marked CANCELLED and the reschedule email is sent before the calendar/video event deletions complete, and any failure to delete is an unhandled rejection invisible to the surrounding try/catch. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` with individual error handling.

requestReschedule no longer awaits calendar/video deletions

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` was introduced because `getCalendar` became async. Since forEach doesn't await its callbacks, the mutation sends the reschedule email, fires webhooks, and returns while the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls are still pending; a serverless function may be frozen before they finish, leaving stale events on users' calendars, and any errors become unhandled rejections. Await the deletions with `Promise.all(...map(...))`.

Recurring-cancellation branch pushes into apiDeletes asynchronously after it is awaited

In the recurring-event cancellation path, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes deletion promises into `apiDeletes` from async callbacks. `apiDeletes` is later consumed by `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (and by `await apiDeletes` in the paid branch), both of which run before any of these pushes happen, so the recurring calendar event deletions are never awaited and their results/errors are lost. Cancel can return success while the recurring events remain on the calendar. Collect the deletions with `Promise.all(credentials.map(...))` and push the resulting promises synchronously.

appStore values are now Promises; only 6 of its consumers were updated

Every entry in the default-exported `appStore` map changed from a module namespace object to a `Promise` via top-level `import(...)`. This is a breaking contract change for every consumer of `@calcom/app-store`, but the PR only updates `getCalendar.ts`, `videoClient.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts`, `bookings.tsx`, `deletePayment.ts`, and `handlePayment.ts`. Any other file that indexes `appStore[...]` synchronously (e.g. `appStore[appName].lib` or `appStore[key].app`) will now receive a Promise and silently fail checks like `"lib" in app` or crash on property access. The change needs an audit (and ideally a type-level guarantee) that all importers of `@calcom/app-store` await the values.

Debug log of CalendarService constructor left in getCalendar

`log.info("calendarApp", calendarApp.lib.CalendarService)` logs the CalendarService class constructor on every calendar resolution. This runs on every booking/availability call, adding noisy, low-value log output (and potentially expensive serialization of a class). It looks like a debugging leftover and should be removed or downgraded.

Locale-stripping regex character class also matches [ \\ ] ^ _

The pattern `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties` uses the character class `[a-zA-Z-_]`, where `Z-_` is a range that also includes the characters `[`, `\`, `]`, `^`, and `_`. It would be safer to use an explicit class like `[a-zA-Z_-]` or to derive the English file name from the file name only rather than from the whole absolute path.

removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete federated recovery-code credentials

The lookup was changed to RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which now also returns credentials from federated user storage (getFederatedCredentialsStream). However, when all codes are used the code still calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...), which only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage. For a user whose recovery codes live in a federated user storage, the removal silently does nothing: the 'all codes used' credential persists in the user storage, and every subsequent login will keep re-adding the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action while the stale credential remains. The deletion path needs to handle federated credentials (e.g., via disableCredentialType/updateCredential on the user storage) or skip removal when the credential is federated.

Used recovery codes in user storage are never consumed, allowing replay

createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the raw generated codes (JSON-serialized plaintext list) in the user storage via UserCredentialModel. Unlike the local keycloak-recovery-authn-codes provider, whose isValid() marks a code as used and persists the updated credential, a federated user storage only validates the presented code against the stored list (see BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid, which does anyMatch without removing anything). Because no updated credential is written back after a successful authentication, a recovery code stored in user storage remains valid forever and can be reused by anyone who has seen it, defeating the one-time-use semantics of recovery codes. Additionally, the codes are transmitted to and held by the user storage as plaintext rather than the hashed form used in local storage, which weakens the at-rest protection for federated stores.

The caller in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS then throws only a misleading 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2'. Since the decoder is only meant to handle DER (which forbids indefinite lengths), readSequence should throw an IOException when readLength() returns -1 to fail loudly on malformed input.

New abstract method order() breaks all external CryptoProvider implementations

Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (the interface is explicitly designed for pluggable crypto integrations, e.g. custom FIPS providers) will now fail to compile or throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when the new CryptoIntegration sorting calls order(). Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 100; }`) would preserve compatibility while still allowing the built-in providers to override it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it.

Additionally the test only asserts that derToRS(rsToDer(x)) == x; it never verifies the produced DER against a Signature.verify() or a known-good JWS vector, so a systematically wrong encoding that round-trips would go undetected. Verifying the re-encoded DER with java.security.Signature (initialized with the matching curve key) would make the test meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process is always False for spawn processes, so hung/dead flusher processes are never killed

The flusher explicitly creates processes with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn"), so the objects are SpawnProcess instances. However, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the *default* context's class (ForkProcess on Linux), and SpawnProcess does not subclass it. Therefore `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` (line 254) and in `join` (line 346) evaluates to False for every flusher process, and `process.kill()` / `process.terminate()` are silently never executed. Consequences: when a flusher process hangs, `_ensure_processes_alive` spawns a replacement without killing the hung one, leaving two processes flushing the same shards and producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic; and on shutdown, processes are never terminated and linger as (daemon) zombies until interpreter exit. The old single-process code had the same latent isinstance bug in `join`, but the new restart path makes it load-bearing. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or just call kill/terminate unconditionally, or track which entries are threads vs processes).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: flusher processes created with the spawn context are SpawnProcess instances that fail the isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process, preventing hung processes from being killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of the process-wait loop on deadline, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes

In `join`, if the deadline is exhausted while waiting for one process, the `break` exits the for-loop over `self.processes` entirely, so none of the remaining processes get `process.terminate()` called (the terminate happens per-iteration after the wait). Previously there was only one process so this couldn't happen. With multiple flusher processes, a slow-to-stop process causes all later processes to be left running after join returns. The terminate should be applied to every remaining process even after the deadline, or the loop should continue with zero remaining time so terminate still runs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that breaking out of the process loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart limit check allows MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS + 1 restarts per process

`if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` is checked before incrementing, so the RuntimeError only fires on the 12th unhealthy detection (restarts 0..10 are permitted, i.e. 11 restarts) even though the constant is named MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10. This was inherited from the previous single-process code but is now duplicated per process; with N processes the consumer tolerates 11*N restarts before crashing. Default --flusher-processes=1 contradicts the stated goal of one flusher process per shard

The new CLI option defaults to 1, meaning a default deployment of process-spans gets a single flusher process shared across all shards via `flusher_processes` being passed to SpanFlusher. But the PR description says the intent is to "spawn a process per redis shard", and SpanFlusher's own default when max_processes is None is `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (one process per shard). Because the click default (1) is always passed, the SpanFlusher default is effectively unreachable from the CLI. If per-shard processes are the intended default, the click default should be None (or omitted) so SpanFlusher falls back to one process per shard.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

Both `age` and `timestamp` are integers where 0 is a legitimate value (age of 0 milliseconds, epoch timestamp 0). A report containing both `timestamp` and `age: 0` (or `timestamp: 0` and `age`) will pass validation even though the spec says they are mutually exclusive, because `0` is falsy. false_positives.candidate:
Chronological merge compares error event timestamps against segment event timestamps with a silent 0 default

In `gen_request_data`, the code interleaves error log messages with breadcrumb log messages by comparing `error_events[error_idx]['timestamp'] < event.get('timestamp', 0)`. Segment events that lack a `timestamp` key default to 0, which causes all remaining error messages to be flushed before those events regardless of when the errors actually occurred, silently corrupting the chronological ordering sent to Seer. Additionally, the two timestamp sources (nodestore event `timestamp` and recording-segment event `timestamp`) are assumed to be on the same clock/units; if they differ, the merged ordering will be wrong. At minimum, events without a timestamp should be handled explicitly instead of defaulting to 0.

get_environment_info performs a recommended-event lookup per issue when building PR comments

Each call hits the eventstore/nodestore, so generating one comment issues a sequence of per-issue queries inline in the PR comment task. If the recommended event lookup is expensive or times out, comment delivery is delayed (the broad `except Exception` also masks real failures by design, so problems will be invisible). Consider batching the event fetches or using a cheaper source of the environment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and the incoming cursor has a negative offset (which any client can supply via a cursor string like `0:-5:0`, parsed by Cursor.from_string), the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. The comment claims 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but this is false: Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. Since the audit log endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers/admins, any such user supplying a negative-offset cursor gets a 500 instead of a BadPaginationError or a clamped offset.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in OptimizedCursorPaginator: applying negative slice offsets to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative indexing and raises AssertionError. The candidate adds triggering conditions and endpoint impact without changing the underlying issue.

organization_context.member can be None for superusers

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `.member` unconditionally via the `or` chain — actually Python short-circuits when is_superuser is True, but a non-superuser whose RpcUserOrganizationContext has `member=None` (e.g. access via org auth token or other non-member paths that this endpoint permits through OrganizationAuditPermission) will hit `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` and get a 500 on every request to this endpoint, even when not requesting optimized pagination. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unchecked dereference of organization_context.member when it is None for org-token or other non-member authentication, causing an AttributeError despite passing permissions. Its title and claim about requests without optimized pagination differ, but the underlying bug matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling is numeric but the endpoint orders by datetime

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` / `math.ceil(value)` on the sort key, which only works for numeric values. The audit logs endpoint uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a datetime object and `math.floor(datetime)` raises a TypeError. The endpoint previously used DateTimePaginator, which converts the datetime to a millisecond timestamp. As written, the 'optimized' path will fail with a 500 on the first page that has results (build_cursor always calls get_item_key). OptimizedCursorPaginator needs the DateTimePaginator key conversion (or should subclass it).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key applies numeric math.floor/ceil operations to a datetime sort key because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets, changing prev-cursor semantics

The change in BasePaginator.get_result replaces `results = queryset[offset:stop]` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, a negative offset was previously impossible to reach successfully (Django would raise), so clamping changes behavior silently for all users of Paginator/DateTimePaginator codebase-wide: a client-supplied negative-offset cursor that used to fail loudly now returns the first page as if offset were 0, while the cursor arithmetic later (`_build_next_values` uses the raw `cursor.offset`) still computes next offsets from the original negative offset, producing inconsistent cursors. If clamping is intended, it should be applied uniformly (and probably rejected with BadPaginationError instead), not papered over only in the slice.

enable_advanced_features passed through self.paginate may not reach the paginator

The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. Sentry's base `Endpoint.paginate` only forwards a fixed set of arguments when constructing the paginator; arbitrary extra kwargs are not passed to the paginator constructor in the standard implementation. If that is the case here, the paginator will always be constructed with `enable_advanced_features=False` (or paginate will raise TypeError for the unexpected kwarg), and the new code path is dead. This needs a test verifying the flag actually reaches OptimizedCursorPaginator.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized audit log path

This PR adds a new paginator (~90 lines) with non-trivial boundary logic (negative offsets, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, cursor building) and a new branch in the audit logs endpoint, but includes no tests. Given that both the datetime key handling and the negative-slice behavior are broken as noted, unit tests covering first-page, next-page, prev-page, and malformed-cursor cases for OptimizedCursorPaginator, plus an endpoint test with optimized_pagination=true, are required before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which serialized builds. Now the lock is only taken when inserting into the cache, and getOrCreateIndex in search.go has no per-key locking (its own TODO acknowledges this). Two concurrent requests (or a request plus a watch event) for the same NamespacedResource can both see GetIndex return nil, both run a full bleve build, and both assign b.cache[key] — the loser's index is never closed (file handles/disk for file-backed indexes leak) and duplicate work is done. A per-key build mutex or singleflight is needed to keep the finer-grained locking safe.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu locking from the entire BuildIndex function to only the cache assignment allows concurrent goroutines to build the same expensive index for the same key. The candidate adds consequences and mitigation without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes b.cache[key] under cacheMu at line 138 and GetIndex reads under RLock. Previously BuildIndex held cacheMu for its whole duration, so writes only happened while no other BuildIndex was running, but TotalDocs was still unsafe — and this PR makes it worse by calling TotalDocs from searchSupport.init's new log line and by allowing concurrent builds. A concurrent map read and write panics at runtime. TotalDocs should take b.cacheMu.RLock() while iterating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while concurrent BuildIndex calls may write to it, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate also connects the risk to the new TotalDocs call in searchSupport.init.

false_positives.candidate:
Data races on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed inside errgroup goroutines

In searchSupport.init, each goroutine spawned by group.Go writes to the outer shared variables: `totalBatchesIndexed++` (line 189) and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` (line 190). These run concurrently with up to initWorkers goroutines and with the main goroutine which reads/overwrites `err` at `err = group.Wait()`. This is an unsynchronized read/write race (flagged by -race) on both `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`, and the span attribute count can be undercounted. Use an atomic counter (or collect per-goroutine) and return the build error only via the goroutine's return value instead of assigning to the shared err.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the cancelable context

NewResourceServer creates ctx/cancel, then calls s.Init(ctx) and returns nil, err on failure without calling cancel(). The background context and its goroutine resources are never released on the error path. Call cancel() before returning the error.
